facts.en: Okra belongs to the mallow family, like hibiscus, and its large yellow flowers with purple centres each last just one day.
Okra pods are picked young, about 7–10 cm long, starting 45–60 days after sowing; fine hairs on the pods can irritate skin, so pickers wear gloves.
Resin from blisters in balsam fir bark has been used to mount specimens on microscope slides and to cement parts of optical instruments together.
New Brunswick made the balsam fir its official tree in 1987; it is famous as a Christmas tree, and its long wood fibres make high-quality paper.
Bhutan fir grows in Himalayan cloud forests at 2,450–4,000 m, all the way up to the timberline, where summers are wet and winters snowy.
Its cones stand upright on the branches and are purple-blue, ripening to a very dark purple; the tree can grow up to 60 m tall.
Around Uluru, Anangu people make spear throwers, spear heads and digging sticks from mulga wood.
What look like its narrow, slightly curved, leathery leaves are phyllodes, which take over the work of making food from sunlight.
From a distance its small, round, golden-yellow flower heads look like tiny pompoms; farmers grow it for shade, animal fodder and green manure.
After the seedling stage, golden wattle has no true leaves; its green 'leaves' are flattened leaf stalks called phyllodes.
Australia's sports teams usually wear green and gold, colours said to come from the wattle's leaves and flowers.
This low perennial grows wild from Chile and western and southern Argentina to the sub-Antarctic islands.
The name palmatum means 'hand-shaped', for its leaves with five to nine lobes; acer is the Latin for 'sharp'.
Long grown by Japanese gardeners, it now has a great many garden forms, whose leaves turn yellow, bronze, purple or red in autumn.

notes.PRK: Kew's checklist places this maple's wild range in south-western Korea and in Japan; it counts North and South Korea as one region.

facts.en: Sugar maples are tapped in early spring; their sap is about 2.5% sugar, so roughly 34 litres are boiled down for each litre of maple syrup.
Its five-lobed leaves turn brilliant red, orange or yellow in autumn, and a tree can be tapped for syrup once it is about 40 years old.
Kiwifruit grows wild in China, where it was called yang tao; a Whanganui teacher, Isabel Fraser, brought its seeds to New Zealand in 1904.
Once sold as the 'Chinese gooseberry', it was renamed kiwifruit in 1959, after a US importer said the fruit needed a new name.

notes.NZL: Kew lists kiwifruit as native to China; it was brought to New Zealand by people.

facts.en: Baobab flowers are waxy white, up to 20 cm across, and hang down from the branches; bats are their main pollinators.
The genus name honours Michel Adanson, a French botanist who lived in Senegal for six years; 'digitata' means hand-shaped, after its leaves.

notes.COM: Kew lists the baobab as native to tropical and southern Africa and southern Arabia, and as brought by people to the Comoros.

facts.en: Some very large Grandidier's baobabs have trunks made of several stems arranged in a ring, and they are largely hollow inside.
Radiocarbon dating shows that Grandidier's baobabs can live for more than 1,000 years.
Australia's boab is a close relative of the baobabs of Africa and Madagascar; its big seed pods probably floated across the sea to north-west Australia.
Its swollen trunk is packed with soft, fibrous wood that stores water for dry times; Aboriginal people ate its seeds and made twine and nets from its fibres.
The Za baobab keeps water stored in its trunk and uses it to put out new leaves in the dry season, before the rains arrive.
People eat its pleasantly sour fruit pulp and its oily seeds, and its trunk has sometimes been hollowed out to hold water.
The gum around bael seeds, plentiful in unripe fruit, is used as household glue and is even mixed into lime plaster to waterproof wells.
In Hindu worship, bael leaves are an essential offering to Lord Shiva; in India the fruit pulp is also beaten with milk and sugar into sherbet.
Native to the Balkan Peninsula, the horse chestnut reached Britain from Turkey in the late 1500s and is now common in parks and streets.
Its seeds, called conkers, grow inside spiky green cases; children in Britain use them in a game of conkers, recorded since 1848.
This spice plant grows from underground rhizomes and is native from West Africa south to Angola.
Its purple flowers turn into pods up to 7 cm long, packed with reddish-brown seeds that taste sharp and peppery.
Tāne Mahuta, a kauri in Waipoua Forest in Northland, is about 1,500 years old and 51.5 m tall, with a trunk 13.77 m around.
Young kauri grow as slim cones; with age they shed their lower branches, leaving a clean, straight trunk. Early sailors found young kauri trunks ideal for ship masts.
Pacific kauri resin was traditionally used to seal canoes, light torches and glaze pots, and soot from burnt resin was used for tattoos.
These trees can live for 300 to 1,000 years, and in Fiji the Pacific kauri is the totem tree of several clans, villages and districts.
Its leaves can be 1 to 2 metres long, edged with prickles and tipped with sharp spines, and its flowering stalk can stand 5 to 8 metres tall.
On Aruba and its neighbouring Dutch Caribbean islands, this agave has long been planted as a living hedge.
Legend says St David had his soldiers wear leeks in their helmets in a battle against the Saxons; by 1536 the leek was tied to St David's Day.
In 2022 the Welsh Leek won protected geographical indication (PGI) status, joining products such as Welsh Lamb and Anglesey Sea Salt.

notes.GBR: Kew lists the leek as a cultivated plant that came from Iran; it was brought to Britain by people.

facts.en: Young desert oaks grow tall and slim; older trees spread a wide crown and grow thick, corky bark that shields them from fire.
Desert oaks grow very slowly, and many of the big trees around Uluru are probably more than 1,000 years old.
Its upright branches bristle with stout spines, and a pair of thick, fleshy little leaves grows just below each spine.
Its wood, known locally as fantsilotra, is sawn into rough planks for village houses and made into boxes and crates.
The bitter aloe grows 2 to 3 m tall on a single stem, and its old dead leaves stay on, hanging round the stem like a skirt.
From May to August its branched flower heads draw sunbirds and weavers, while monkeys and baboons raid them for nectar.
Its leaves grow in a perfect spiral, turning clockwise or anticlockwise, in five rows of 15 to 30 leaves; one plant has about 150 leaves.
It grows wild in cracks on steep basalt slopes high in Lesotho's mountains, 2,000 to 2,500 m up, often in mist and sometimes under winter snow.
Aloe vera was brought to Aruba in 1840; its farming made the island prosperous, and an aloe plant is shown on Aruba's coat of arms.
DNA studies place the wild home of aloe vera on the Arabian Peninsula, at the northern edge of the aloes' range; the genus began in southern Africa.

notes.ABW: Kew lists aloe vera as native to the Arabian Peninsula (northern Oman) and brought by people to Aruba, where it has been farmed since the 1800s.
notes.CUW: Kew lists aloe vera as native to the Arabian Peninsula (northern Oman) and as brought by people to the island.

facts.en: Samoa's Teuila Festival takes its name from red ginger, and the flowers are used for decorations across the islands during festival week.
Its red, cone-shaped flower head is made of overlapping bracts; the true flowers are small, white and tube-shaped.

notes.WSM: Kew lists red ginger as native from the Moluccas and New Guinea to Vanuatu and New Caledonia, and as brought by people to Samoa.

facts.en: Māori marked forest trails by snapping silver fern fronds and turning them over, so their silvery-white undersides pointed the way like arrows.
The silver fern took on its role as a national symbol with the New Zealand Natives rugby tour of 1888–1889.
Large cardamom flowers open around 5:30 in the morning, and big-bodied bumblebees are their main pollinators, while honeybees mostly just take the pollen.
The cashew nut is the true fruit; the juicy 'cashew apple' above it is really the swollen stalk, eaten fresh or made into juice.
Portuguese traders took the cashew from north-east Brazil to Mozambique and India's coast in the 1500s, where it was planted to stop soil erosion.
A pineapple forms when 100 to 200 small berries fuse as they grow, giving one fruit with a tough rind made of six-sided units.
A new plant can be grown from the leafy crown cut from the top of the fruit, though it takes at least two years to flower.

notes.ATG: Kew lists the pineapple as native from Costa Rica to tropical South America; it was brought to Antigua by people.

facts.en: When it dries out, its branches curl up. Rain makes them open again within about two hours, and raindrops then knock the seeds out of its fruits.
Fruits on the outside open before those deeper inside, which need heavier rain, so its seeds are released in step with the rainfall.
Despite its name, the poppy anemone belongs to the buttercup family; coronaria means "crown", after the crown at the centre of its flower.
In spring each stem carries a single red, blue or white flower with a black centre, and after flowering the plant dies back.
Garden angelica belongs to the carrot family; its roots, seeds, leaves and young stems all taste rather like liquorice.
Its name archangelica comes from an old belief that an archangel showed people the value of the plant; it thrives in cool places near running water.
Charles Darwin saw its long nectar spur and predicted an insect with a tongue long enough to reach the nectar; decades later, such a sphinx moth was found.
Its name sesquipedale means 'one and a half feet', after its spur of up to 45 cm; the creamy white flowers release a strong scent at night.
Its name, kangaroo paw, comes from the shape of the cluster of flowers before they open; it is the floral emblem of Western Australia.
The woolly flowers are deep red at the base and bright green above, and birds visit them for nectar, pollinating them.
Peanut plants flower above ground but ripen their pods below it, which is why the species is named hypogaea, 'under the earth'.
Like many legumes, peanut roots carry nodules of nitrogen-fixing bacteria, so the crop enriches the soil it grows in.
Prized for its good timber, the Parana pine was logged so heavily that its natural forests were close to exhausted by the late 1980s.
It behaves partly like a pioneer species: it regrows naturally in its own forests and often spreads into open grassland.
Indigenous peoples of Chile and Argentina gather its large seeds for food and grind them into flour; some regard the tree as sacred.
Its stiff, triangular leaves end in a sharp, spiny tip and can stay on the tree for 10 to 15 years.
Bunya cones are as big as footballs and hold 50 to 100 large seeds, called bunya nuts; heavy crops come about every three years.
In good years, Aboriginal groups from far away gathered at the Bunya Mountains for the nuts, with ceremonies, law-making and the passing on of lore.
Cook pines lean towards the equator, the whole tree from base to crown, and trees farther from the equator lean more; the reason is not well understood.
On Captain Cook's second voyage, New Caledonia's Isle of Pines was named for these trees, which almost covered the island.
Norfolk Island pines can grow 60 m tall; their seeds drop in May and June, feeding the endangered green parrot.
Every 5 to 7 years the trees make a huge crop of seeds, and the forest floor fills with seedlings.
Breadfruit can be eaten at every stage: firm, mature fruit is cooked as a starchy staple, and soft, ripe fruit has sweet, creamy flesh.
In the late 1700s, seedless breadfruit from Tahiti was taken to Jamaica and St Vincent; these Polynesian varieties later spread to Africa, India and South-East Asia.
Cut any living part of a jackfruit tree and it oozes a sticky white latex, which people have used to mend broken pots and seal leaky boats.
Jackfruit wood resists termites and rot and polishes well, so it is used for furniture and musical instruments; its heartwood chips give a yellow dye for monks' robes.

notes.BGD: Kew lists the jackfruit as native to India, and as brought by people to Bangladesh.
notes.LKA: Kew lists the jackfruit as native to India, and as brought by people to Sri Lanka.

facts.en: To make rooibos tea, young branches are cut, chopped and bruised, then left in heaps to 'sweat', which turns them reddish brown and sweet.
The tea comes mainly from forms of this needle-leaved shrub that grow in South Africa's Cederberg Mountains, whose indigenous people used it long before it became popular.
About four-fifths of okoumé timber is peeled into thin sheets for plywood, and its light wood is also used in boat building.
In Gabon and Equatorial Guinea, resin from its bark is burnt for light in torches and lamps.
Oats were domesticated much later than wheat and barley; for a long time wild oats grew as weeds in the fields of those crops.
As farming spread across Europe, its cooler, wetter climate probably suited oats, which are now grown widely in north-west Europe.
Grey mangroves send up spongy, pencil-like roots from their underground roots; these poke up through the mud so that the roots can breathe.
It keeps out much of the salt at its roots and gets rid of the rest through salt glands on its leaves, mostly on their grey undersides.
Neem seeds contain azadirachtin, a natural compound that puts insects off their food and upsets their growth, so farmers use neem sprays to protect crops.
Neem wood resists termites, so it is used for fence posts, and cupboards made from it help keep insects away from what is stored inside.

notes.IND: Kew lists neem as native only in its Assam region; elsewhere in India it was brought by people.

facts.en: This low subshrub grows wild in the Magellan region at the southern tip of South America and on sub-Antarctic islands.
Common bamboo is a giant grass: a new cane shoots up to its full 10 to 20 metres in about three months, sometimes gaining 20 cm in a day.
Its cut canes take root very easily: in Jamaica, whole stands of bamboo grew from green canes that farmers had pushed into the ground as yam stakes.

notes.LCA: Kew lists common bamboo as native from north-east India to southern China and Indo-China, and as brought by people to Saint Lucia.

facts.en: Its other name, saw banksia, comes from its saw-edged leaves; its big yellow-green flower spikes are made of many tiny flowers that birds and insects visit.
After a bushfire, new shoots appear along its thick bark within about a week, and the heat helps its tough seed heads split open.
Its large, fluffy flowers, packed with white stamens tipped with pink, open around sunset; fruit bats and night-flying moths pollinate them.
Its box-shaped fruit, up to 10 cm wide, has a tough, corky husk that helps it float, so it is spread by water.
The Hong Kong orchid tree is sterile, so every new tree has to be grown from a cutting, a graft or by air-layering.
DNA studies have confirmed that it is a hybrid of two other bauhinias, the purple camel's foot and the camel's foot tree.
The daisy's Latin name, Bellis, comes from Latin for 'pretty'; garden daisies often spread into lawns, where many people see them as weeds.
About 53,000 people voted in the 2023 Dutch poll that chose the daisy; the tulip was left out because it does not grow wild in the Netherlands.
Brazil nuts are gathered from wild trees in the Amazon rainforest, and this harvest has helped protect millions of hectares of forest.
Each hard, woody pod holds 15 to 25 seeds, the 'nuts'; the tree may live for centuries and grow taller than 40 m.
Sugar beet was bred from white Silesian beet, a fodder crop with about 4–6% sugar; from the late 1700s, selection raised its sugar to over 18%.
Sugar beet, beetroot, chard and the wild sea beet are all forms of one species; sugar beet probably came from the wild sea beet through breeding.
Saskatchewan made the paper birch its official tree in 1988; First Nations made canoes, baskets and utensils from its papery white bark.
Paper birch grows fast but rarely lives beyond 140 years; its light, winged seeds can blow a long way across the surface of snow.
Silver birch can improve soil: its spreading roots draw up nutrients, which return to the ground surface when the tree drops its leaves.
Birch bark has been used to make roofs, baskets and even shoes, and at Midsummer many Finns stand two young birches by their door.
In Greenland these birches are usually 4 to 5 metres tall, occasionally almost 10 metres, with thick, crooked trunks.
In a few sheltered valleys of South Greenland, such as Qinngua near Tasermiut Fjord, dense stands of these birches look like a real forest.
Himalayan birch bark peels off in thin sheets, and its inner bark has been used as paper, mainly for writing religious texts.
Its species name utilis means 'useful', for the many uses of its hard wood and other parts; it is a sacred plant in the Himalaya.
As the rainy season ends, near the Ethiopian New Year in September, the land turns yellow with Adey Abeba daisies, and girls in new clothes give friends bouquets.
Annatto seeds carry bright orange-red coats, and the dye made from them is used to colour food, especially dairy products.
Its fruit is a capsule covered in long bristles, and Indigenous peoples of the Americas have used the red seed dye as paint.
The name ackee comes from 'ankye' in the Twi language of Ghana; the tree was brought to Jamaica from West Africa, probably aboard a slave ship.
When ripe, the red and yellow pods burst open to show shiny black seeds on yellow arils, which are cooked for ackee and saltfish, Jamaica's national dish.

notes.JAM: Kew lists the ackee as native to West Africa and brought by people to Jamaica.

facts.en: Palms older than about 25 years develop a bulge in the trunk, some two-thirds of the way up.
Its trunks resist rot and termites, so they are used as posts and for bridges, while young leaves are woven into mats and baskets.
Its sweet sap is collected by tapping the flower stalks and made into palm sugar, which can be used instead of cane sugar.
Flabellifer means 'fan-bearing', after its stiff, fan-shaped leaves, up to 3 m across, on stalks edged with hard spines.

notes.THA: Kew lists the palmyra palm as brought by people to Thailand; it is native in nearby Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and Viet Nam.

facts.en: Frankincense is the resin of this tree. In Wadi Dawkah in Oman, frankincense trees still grow along the valley floor and their resin is harvested to this day.
Frankincense was a prized luxury of the ancient world: caravans carried it from the valleys of Dhofar to coastal ports such as Khor Rori.
Its tiny real flowers are usually white; the bright pink, purple or red parts around them are bracts, which are modified leaves.
A woody climber armed with curved thorns, it needs a fence, wall or pergola to lean on, and once settled it copes well with drought.

notes.GUM: Bougainvillea, Guam's territorial flower, is grown in gardens there; Kew's checklist has no record of it on Guam.

facts.en: Around October it often drops its leaves, so the whole tree stands bare but covered in bright red, bell-shaped flowers.
Its name acerifolius means 'maple-leaved': its lobed leaves look like those of some maples.
Msasa trees are known for their spring leaves, which open copper, bronze, pink and deep red before turning dark green.
Its flat, woody pods split open explosively to scatter the seeds, and bees visiting its flowers make an excellent honey.
The name canola joins 'Canada', where it was bred, and 'ola' for oil; canola is rapeseed whose oil has under 2% erucic acid.
Its small yellow flowers turn into pods like pea pods, each holding tiny black seeds that are about 45% oil.
Cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and Brussels sprouts are all forms of this one species.
Wild cabbage grows on sea cliffs in southern England and on other Atlantic coasts of Europe; people began growing it about 5,000 years ago.
Palash often flowers while its branches are bare of leaves, covering the tree in bright orange; birds are its main pollinators.
Its flowers yield a yellow to orange-red dye used on silk, and in India it is a major host tree for the lac insect, which makes shellac.
Its showy flowers have long stamens and a long style, and one of the five petals is smaller than the other four.
Two of its flowers are shown on the golden shield of Barbados's coat of arms, next to a bearded fig tree.

notes.BRB: Kew lists the pride of Barbados as native from south-eastern Mexico to Central America, and as brought by people to Barbados.

facts.en: Arta has long taproots that reach down to water and help hold sand dunes in place, so it is also planted as a barrier against the spreading desert.
In spring it bears small white, yellowish or red flowers, followed by oval fruits covered in hairs; in the UAE its young twigs and fruits are eaten.
Its genus name, Calluna, probably comes from a Greek word meaning 'to sweep clean', because heather was used to make brooms.
Heather forms thick mats of tiny, scale-like leaves, with spikes of pink to purple flowers in mid to late summer.
This seashore tree stands up to strong wind, salt spray and drought, so it is planted along coasts to shelter land and hold the soil.
Oil from its round nuts was burned in lamps by some Polynesians, and it is also used as a finish for wooden bowls.
Its seeds carry tufts of silky white hairs that are used to stuff mattresses and pillows, and its stems give a strong fibre for ropes and fishing nets.
It thrives in dry, salty ground and quickly spreads over degraded roadsides, abandoned fields and overgrazed pastures, so it is taken as a sign of overused land.
Despite its name, the marsh marigold is not related to garden marigolds and looks nothing like them; it belongs to the buttercup family.
It needs constant moisture, so it grows at pond edges and in boggy ground, and its bright yellow flowers open early in spring.
Nicaragua's 1971 law making the madroño its national tree also ordered it planted in parks, squares and along roads, and at every school on Arbor Day.
Its hard, smooth, yellowish wood, sold as degame or lemonwood, has been used for carving, fishing rods and archery bows.
Green, oolong and black teas all come from this one plant: they differ mainly in how far the picked leaves are left to oxidise before drying.
There are two main kinds of tea plant: the small-leaved Chinese variety and the larger-leaved Assam variety from India.
Harebells look delicate but are tough, growing in dry, open places from bare hill slopes and mountain tops to sand dunes and windswept coasts.
In Scotland the harebell is called the bluebell; its round leaves grow at the base, while the leaves up its thin stem are very narrow.
Crush a leaf or twig of this tree and it smells of camphor; its wood, leaves and twigs are a commercial source of camphor.
This large evergreen tree is valued in Asia for its timber and for the oils taken from it.
Its flowers open dull green and turn yellow as they age; they yield a perfume oil that is also used in soaps and cosmetics.
In forests the tree can grow 40 m tall, but trees grown for perfume are usually no more than 3 m high.

notes.COM: Kew lists ylang-ylang as brought by people to the Comoros; it is native from South-East Asia to Queensland in Australia.
notes.SYC: Kew lists ylang-ylang as brought by people to Seychelles; it is native from South-East Asia to Queensland in Australia.

facts.en: The Incas held the cantuta sacred and carried it as a symbol of their achievements and conquests.
Bolivia's decree on state symbols describes the kantuta as a bell-shaped Andean flower in red, yellow and green, the colours of the national flag.
Capers are the flower buds of this bush, picked by hand before they open while still small and dark green, then dried and kept in salt or vinegar.
Buds left on the bush open into white flowers with long purple stamens that last just one day, followed by oblong fruits called caper berries.
Sweet peppers and hot chillies belong to this one species, whose many varieties differ in size, colour, shape and heat.
Chilli belongs to the nightshade family and is native to the Americas, from south-western North America to northern South America.
Papaya is a giant herb rather than a true tree: its single stem is soft, not woody, and carries the scars of old leaves.
Papain, an enzyme from the milky sap of young papayas, is used to make meat tender, and the peppery black seeds can stand in for black pepper.
Saguaros grow very slowly: in Saguaro National Park their arms normally appear at 50 to 70 years of age, and in drier places it can take 100 years.
After heavy rain a saguaro soaks up water and its pleats spread out like an accordion; in dry spells it lives on the stored water and the pleats shrink back.
Pequi flowers open at night and are visited by bats and moths; in the morning birds drink the leftover nectar, and one study in central Brazil counted 13 kinds.
While the Cerrado's peak flowering comes in the rainy season, the pequi flowers in the dry season, with up to 30 flowers in each cluster.
When amaltas blooms, the tree is often almost bare of leaves and hung with long, drooping chains of bright yellow flowers, 30–60 cm long.
Its round pods, 40–60 cm long, hang from the branches without splitting open; inside, thin cross walls divide each pod into rooms for up to 100 seeds.

notes.THA: Kew lists the golden shower tree as native to India and Sri Lanka, and as brought by people to Thailand.

facts.en: Unlike horse chestnut seeds, sweet chestnuts are good to eat: they are roasted or used in cooking, and the Romans ground them into flour.
Its nuts grow in prickly green cases; the ancient Greeks dedicated the tree to Zeus, and its name Castanea may come from a Greek town, Castonis.
It probably comes from a small area of south-eastern Madagascar, but it is now planted, and grows wild, all over the tropics.
In warm places it flowers and fruits all year round, and a seedling can start flowering 6 to 8 weeks after it sprouts.
William Cattley flowered this orchid in Britain in 1818, and the botanist John Lindley named it Cattleya labiata after him in 1821.
For about 70 years after its discovery, collectors could not find it in the wild: they searched near Rio de Janeiro instead of Pernambuco, where it grows.
It is named after Mrs Moss, an English orchid grower in whose collection it flowered in 1836.
Wild plants grow high in the forest canopy at 900 to 1,500 m, and more than a century of collecting has put the orchid in danger.
This orchid is endangered: in some regions it has lost 80% of its habitat in the last 100 years, and wild plants have been heavily collected.
Colombia named 2010 its National Year of Orchids, the family of this flower; the country has about 3,500 orchid species.
The Atlas cedar grows wild in the mountains of Morocco and Algeria. It is endangered: logging, fires and grazing goats have shrunk its forests.
Atlas cedars grow between about 1,300 and 2,600 metres up; about four-fifths of their forest is in the Middle Atlas of Morocco.
Deodar heartwood is very durable, with a distinct smell and an oily feel, and is widely used for buildings, railway sleepers and furniture.
Deodar often grows in pure forests on cool, north-facing Himalayan slopes, and it is planted to hold the soil against erosion.
In ancient times, cedar of Lebanon timber was prized for building ships and grand places of worship.
The cedar of Lebanon is listed as Vulnerable; an estimate from the 1990s put the remaining original forest in Lebanon and Syria at about 5%.
Kapok, the fluffy fibre lining its pods, is light, water-repellent and floats, so it has filled life jackets as well as pillows and mattresses.
Its flowers open after dark and give off a strong smell; fruit bats and moths visit them at night, and bees arrive at dawn.

notes.GNQ: Kew lists the kapok tree as native to the tropical Americas and as brought by people to Bioko; Kew does not list it on the mainland.
notes.SLE: Kew lists the kapok tree as native to the tropical Americas and as brought by people to Sierra Leone.

facts.en: Farmers in Africa's Sahel domesticated pearl millet 4,000 to 5,000 years ago; it reached the Indian subcontinent about 3,000 years ago.
In West Africa's dry zone, where just 250 to 400 mm of rain falls a year and heat is fierce, pearl millet is the dominant cereal.

notes.MRT: Kew lists pearl millet as brought by people to Mauritania; in its checklist the crop is native from Benin and Burkina Faso east to Chad and south to Mozambique.
notes.NER: Kew lists pearl millet as brought by people to Niger; in its checklist the crop is native from Benin and Burkina Faso east to Chad and south to Mozambique.

facts.en: Its name comes from 'corn', an old word for grain crops such as wheat, barley and oats, among which cornflowers once grew commonly.
Modern farming caused a dramatic fall in wild cornflowers; in Britain numbers started to recover in the late 1980s on land left unsprayed.

notes.EST: Kew lists the cornflower as native to the eastern Mediterranean; in Estonia it grows wild after being brought by people.

facts.en: Carob pods are sweet; their dried pulp is ground into a powder that is used in place of cocoa.
Carob seeds give locust bean gum, which food makers use to thicken ice cream, sauces and cheese.
Colombian law bans cutting down the wax palm and lets the government buy land in the Cordillera Central, Colombia's central Andean range, for parks protecting it.
Its smooth, upright trunk is coated with a layer of wax, which gives the palm its name, and it can grow up to 60 m tall.
Its Chinese name, hong kuai, means 'red cypress', and the species name formosensis comes from Formosa, an old name for Taiwan.
It grows on the mountains of northern and central Taiwan, 1,000–3,000 metres up, and its crushed leaves smell oddly of rotting seaweed.
This rare, endangered shrub grows wild nowhere but the Maltese Islands, mostly on a few coastal cliffs of Malta and Gozo, and is protected by law.
Malta chose it as its national plant in 1971 because of its rarity, and since 2024 a law on national species gives it stronger protection.
Like the potato, quinoa was a main food of Andean peoples before the Incas; the grain is often roasted and ground into flour for bread.
The United Nations named 2013 the International Year of Quinoa to honour Andean peoples, who kept the crop alive for generations; it is now grown in India too.
Garden chrysanthemums are a complex hybrid of five wild Chinese species; the name morifolium means 'mulberry-leaved', after the shape of the leaves.
Chrysanthemums reached Japan from China in the Nara period (710–794), and the flower is believed to have become the imperial emblem under Emperor Go-Toba.
Chickpea plants are covered in glandular hairs that give off malic and oxalic acids; each small, puffed-up pod holds just one or two seeds.
Chickpeas come in two main types: small-seeded desi and large-seeded kabuli, whose plants are usually taller.

notes.IND: Kew lists the chickpea as native to West Asia, and as brought by people to India.
notes.PAK: Kew lists the chickpea as native to West Asia, and as brought by people to Pakistan.

facts.en: Peru's coat of arms shows a vicuna, a quina tree and a horn of plenty spilling coins, standing for the country's riches in the three natural kingdoms.
Ecuador has 12 kinds of cinchona, woody plants of its Andes at 1,500 to 3,000 m; in 1936 this species was named the country's national plant.
Cinnamon sticks are inner bark: shoots are cut, the bark is peeled off in strips and its outer layer scraped away, and the inner bark curls into quills.
Its other Latin name, Cinnamomum zeylanicum, comes from Ceylon, the old name of Sri Lanka, where the tree is native.
The desert hyacinth is a holoparasite, living wholly off other plants. In Qatar it grows mainly on coastal sands and flowers in March and April.
Colocynth belongs to the same genus as the watermelon. It is a trailing desert vine with fruits about the size of a small orange, striped green and yellow.
A tuberous root lets the colocynth survive in dry lands, and its trailing stems grow up to 3 metres long.
Its finger-shaped fruit grows up to 8 cm long and is filled with pulp that looks like caviar, green to pinkish in colour.
Pomelos are offered as temple fruits and given as lucky gifts at festivals, a custom especially popular in Chinese communities.
Pomelo trees may flower two to four times a year; their strongly scented flowers are made into perfume in northern Viet Nam.
Mandarins have a thin, loose peel that comes off the segments easily, and the fruit takes about 7–10 months to ripen after the tree blooms.
Dried mandarin rind tastes sweet and spicy and is used to flavour cakes, while oil from the peel goes into perfumes.
Nobody has found the sweet orange growing truly wild; it probably arose near the China–Vietnam border.
Little of an orange is wasted: besides the juice and fruit, pulp is fed to cattle, and pectin and fragrant oils are made from the peel.
On windy coasts with poor, dry soil the sea grape stays a sprawling shrub, but planted away from the sea it grows into a small tree.
Its round leaves can be 20 cm wide, and its purple fruits hang in long, tightly packed chains, like bunches of grapes.
On Grand Cayman and Cayman Brac, people once made rope from its leaves; fishermen valued the rope because it lasted well in sea water.
The tops of its round, fan-shaped leaves are dark green, while the undersides look silvery to golden.
Coconut husks give three kinds of fibre: one for mats and yarn, a bristly one for brushes, and one for stuffing mattresses.
Tall coconut palms shed pollen before the same cluster's female flowers are ready, so they are cross-pollinated, mostly by insects and partly by wind.

notes.IND: Kew lists the coconut as brought by people to India.
notes.MDV: Kew lists the coconut palm as brought by people to the Maldives.

facts.en: Arabica means 'of Arabia', yet this coffee does not grow wild there: its native home is south-west Ethiopia, eastern South Sudan and northern Kenya.
India's coffee story is said to begin around 1600, when the saint Baba Budan planted seven 'Mocha' seeds at his hermitage in the hills of Karnataka.
Robusta grows as a shrub or small tree up to 12 m tall, often with several light brown branches instead of a single trunk.
Robusta is native to tropical western and central Africa; it was already being farmed for its beans in what is now DR Congo in the 1870s.
Kola nuts grow in knobbly green pods, and each nut is either red or white.
Across West Africa, kola nuts are shared at ceremonies and social gatherings, and kola trees are often planted among cacao to shade it.
Antarctic pearlwort grows as low cushions or mats, and it is found all the way from Mexico to the Antarctic Peninsula, from sea level to 4,200 m.
Along with Antarctic hair grass, it is one of the two flowering plants native to Antarctica.
Taro is grown for its starchy corm, a staple food sometimes called the 'potato' of the tropics; its name esculenta means 'good to eat'.
Taro must be cooked, dried or soaked in water before it is eaten, which removes harmful substances found in the raw plant.
Each mopane leaf has two leaflets shaped like butterfly wings; in the midday heat they fold together to save water, so the trees cast little shade.
Mopane worms, big caterpillars of an emperor moth, feed on its leaves; people roast or dry them to eat, and selling them brings in useful income.
The St Helena gumwood is a small tree, five to eight metres tall, with an umbrella-like crown and white flower heads that droop from its branch tips.
Gumwood woodland once covered a third of St Helena; to mark the Millennium, a new gumwood forest of over 4,000 trees was planted.
Myrrh is a sturdy, spiny shrub or small tree of open bushland; every branch ends in a spine, and its silvery bark peels off in papery flakes.
Its name Commiphora is Greek for 'gum bearer': cuts in the stem release an aromatic gum-resin that sets hard and yellowish.
Its sweetly scented white flowers hang like tiny bells along one side of the stem, and the scent is a favourite in perfumes.
Its Finnish name, kielo, is also an old girl's name, and Finns often give it to friendly cows too.
Carnauba wax comes from the palm's leaves; it was once made into candles and now goes into cosmetics, cleaning products and coatings for computer chips.
The carnauba palm is native to north-eastern Brazil, where its wax has long been an important export.
Jute fibre comes from the stem's inner bark: bundles of plants soak in slow-flowing water for 12–15 days, then the fibre is pulled off by hand.
Jute was once called the golden fibre of Bangladesh; it is used for hessian and sacking, carpets, canvas and paper.
Its round, woody fruits float easily, so ocean currents carry them from island to island.
In Hawaii its bright orange, funnel-shaped flowers are strung into leis (garlands), and Pacific islanders long carved its wood into cups and bowls.
A young cabbage tree has one slim trunk; it starts to branch after it flowers, and each branch ends in a tuft of long, narrow leaves.
Māori wove its leaves and ate its roots, young shoots and trunk core, which are rich in a sugar called fructose; the trunk and roots were steamed first.
In Hawaii, its tough, shiny leaves, slow to wilt, are used to wrap food for cooking, to thatch roofs and to make hula skirts.
The earliest Polynesian settlers brought the ti plant to Hawaii, where it was sacred and is still planted around homes for good luck.
Pampas grass grows in big clumps topped by tall, silvery-white, feather-like plumes; female plants carry showier plumes than male plants.
Its long, narrow leaves have very sharp, saw-toothed edges, and it has become invasive in parts of the United States.
Hazel flowers before its leaves open: dangling yellow male catkins, like lambs' tails, and tiny red female flowers, which are pollinated by the wind.
Although each tree has both male and female flowers, hazel needs pollen from another hazel tree; each nut grows in a leafy husk that covers about three-quarters of it.
The yellow trumpet is a savanna plant with just four leaves pressed flat against the ground and yellow flowers.
Nigeria's national flower, the yellow trumpet, is shown on the national coat of arms, though there its flowers are painted red.
Its flowers grow on long, tangled branches that sprout from the trunk; the round, woody fruits take about 18 months to ripen and look like rusty cannonballs.
In India it is often planted near Hindu temples and held sacred, as its flower is said to resemble the hooded snake (naga) of Lord Shiva.
Hawthorn blossom marks the turn from spring to summer, and its leaves and flowers were used for May Day garlands.
Thick and thorny, hawthorn has long been planted as hedging; its berries, called haws, feed migrating birds such as redwings and thrushes.
The calabash tree grows its flowers straight from the trunk and old branches; they open in the evening, and bats visit them for nectar.
Its round fruits, up to 30 cm wide, have hard shells that people dry and carve into cups, bowls and maracas.
Unlike spring crocuses, the saffron crocus flowers in autumn; each lavender flower has three red stigmas, which are picked by hand and dried to make saffron.
It takes about 150 to 170 flowers to make one gram of saffron, and all that hand-picking is why the spice is so costly.

notes.IRN: Kew lists saffron as a farmed plant that arose in Greece and was brought by people to Iran.

facts.en: A 2018 study concluded that melons were domesticated more than once, in Africa and in Asia, and found a close relative of the melon in India.
In the Middle Ages, the traveller Ibn Battuta wrote that melons from Konye-Urgench, in today's Turkmenistan, were sliced, dried in the sun and carried to India and China.

notes.TKM: Kew lists the melon as brought by people to Turkmenistan, where growers have bred their own melons for centuries.
notes.UZB: Kew lists the melon as brought by people to Uzbekistan.

facts.en: Tsenden is a tall evergreen tree, 20–45 m high, that rises above the oak-dominated evergreen forests where it grows.
Considered sacred in Bhutan, tsenden is planted beside dzongs and monasteries, and its durable timber resists rot and wood-boring insects.

notes.BTN: A Bhutanese government booklet names the national tree Cupressus torulosa; Kew, BGCI and RBGE place the tsenden in Cupressus cashmeriana.

facts.en: Sarv-e Abarkuh, a cypress in central Iran, stands about 25 metres tall, and experts estimate that it is 4,000 to 5,000 years old.
Its name sempervirens means 'always green'. Its hard, lasting wood keeps its scent long after cutting, and the scent keeps moths away.
Turmeric spice comes from the plant's underground stems (rhizomes), whose bright yellow dye also colours food, fabrics and paints.
Turmeric is called the 'poor man's saffron' because its colour looks like saffron's at a lower price; it is a key ingredient of curry powder.
In Bislama this cycad is called namele, and its leaves have long been a sign of peace in Vanuatu's cultures.
A tabu, a ban on some activity, has long been shown by laying namele leaves on the ground where everyone can see them.
The Cyprus cyclamen is a small plant, 7 to 15 cm tall, with heart-shaped, toothed leaves that are rich purple underneath.
It is one of 23 known species of cyclamen. It is endemic to Cyprus and grows across much of the island.
This small spring orchid has long, narrow leaves; its short flower stalks each bear one to three small, scented flowers, held low among the leaves.
In Chinese art the orchid is one of the 'Four Gentlemen', with plum blossom, chrysanthemum and bamboo; growing in quiet valleys, it stands for a gracious character.
Papyrus is a giant sedge: its smooth green stems grow up to 5 m tall, each topped by a ball of thin stalks like a feather duster.
Ancient Egyptians made paper from its stems, and in deep water papyrus builds the floating, tangled mats of plants known as sudd.
Its strong timber lasts a long time and resists termites; in Singapore some hawkers' big chopping boards are cut from it.
A tembusu tree in the Singapore Botanic Gardens is pictured on the back of Singapore's five-dollar note.
Rimu can grow 60 m tall, and its red-orange, berry-like fruits are an important food for New Zealand's kākāpō.
Rimu was widely used for building houses, and logging has left very few untouched rimu forests in the North Island.
Dahlia coccinea is a simple wild dahlia with few petals that grows in the Mexican countryside; it is a wild ancestor of today's garden dahlias.
This wild flower is an ancestor of today's garden dahlias, of which more than 50,000 varieties have been bred around the world.
Its wood, like that of related trees sold as Madagascar rosewood, is used for fine cabinets and building; the tree has become endangered in eastern Madagascar.
For more than 300 years its fragrant, richly patterned wood has been used for fine furniture, cabinets and pianos.
It grows wild in Brazil alone, in its Atlantic Forest, where centuries of logging and forest clearing have made it rare.
Shisham heartwood is very hard, seasons without warping or splitting and resists dry-wood termites, so it is used for fine furniture.
Shisham grows fast, and trees have reached 11 m in five years; its root nodules and falling leaves enrich the soil with nitrogen.
Its bark gives the fibre for lokta, Nepal's traditional handmade paper; the paper takes its name from lokta, a local name for the bark.
Daphne-bark paper is also made in Bhutan, where it was valued for religious scriptures and historical documents because termites and insects avoid it.
Each small flower head is wrapped by two large white bracts that look like a dove, which gives the tree its name.
It is named after Armand David, a French missionary who collected plants and animals in China in the 1800s; a young tree may take ten years to flower.
Gulmohar is native to Madagascar, but it is now planted along avenues and in gardens across the tropics and subtropics for its flame-red flowers.
Its Latin name Delonix comes from Greek words meaning 'visible claw', after the clawed base of its petals, and regia means 'royal'.
Dendrobium comes from Greek words for 'tree' and 'life', because many of these orchids grow perched on tree trunks and branches.
The Cooktown orchid became Queensland's floral emblem in 1959, after a public poll that drew more than 10,000 entries.
Noble dendrobium grows on trees or rocks; its fragrant, rose-pink flowers, as wide as 5 cm, have a dark purple lip.
From winter into spring its flowers come out of the leafless joints of its stems and last three to six weeks.
Male bamboo's stems have very thick walls and are often solid, especially in dry places, so they are used for scaffolding, bridges, poles and walking sticks.
It grows in dense clumps of stems 8–16 m tall; the stems are a raw material for paper mills, and the young shoots are eaten.
One of Antarctica's two native flowering plants, this grass grows on the Antarctic Peninsula's north and west and on nearby islands that thaw in summer.
This small grass stands just 3 to 20 cm tall; it grows in separate clumps or forms thick carpets of up to several hundred square metres.
This tree fern can grow up to 15 m tall, with a spreading crown of big, dark green fronds up to 6 m across.
In gardens its trunk can carry other ferns, orchids and mosses, and more delicate ferns grow in its shelter.
The St Helena tree fern grows wild on St Helena and nowhere else.
Foxglove's spotted lower lip attracts bees: they land on it and climb up the tube-shaped flower, carrying pollen from other foxgloves.
The 'glove' in foxglove probably comes from its flowers looking like the fingers of a glove; why 'fox' is less certain.
Some fonio varieties ripen just 6 to 8 weeks after planting, ahead of other cereals, so they feed families early in the season.
Its English nickname 'hungry rice' is misleading: farmers grow fonio for its quality, and it can yield even on very poor soils.
Each big yellow flower lasts a single day; the ripe fruit then splits open like a star, showing seeds covered in red flesh.
Its large leaves serve as food wrappers, for tempeh for example, or are folded into cones to hold rojak.
Venus flytraps grow wild in coastal North Carolina and a small area of north-eastern South Carolina; muscipula is Latin for 'little mousetrap'.
Each trap has six trigger hairs: when an insect or spider brushes two of them, the hinged halves snap shut, and the trap reopens after digesting its prey.
The Guinea yam comes from West Africa; its starchy tubers are a staple across a belt of land stretching from Côte d'Ivoire to Cameroon.
Its twining vine can grow up to 12 m long, so farmers put up stakes for it to climb a month or two after the shoots appear.
Kaki is the persimmon's Japanese name, and Diospyros comes from Greek words often read as 'divine fruit' or 'wheat of Zeus'.
Persimmon trees can set seedless fruit without pollination, and ripe fruit often hangs on the bare branches after the leaves have fallen.
Its thick branches spread into an umbrella-shaped crown, and its upward-facing leaves gather water from the mists that drift over Socotra's high plateaus.
Its deep red resin, called dragon's blood, is harvested once or twice a year; on Socotra it is used to paint pottery and as nail varnish and make-up.
When its bark is cut, the dragon tree oozes a red resin known as dragon's blood.
Several unrelated plants give a red 'dragon's blood' resin, including a close relative of this tree that grows on Socotra, a Yemeni island in the Arabian Sea.
Mountain avens is a low, creeping dwarf shrub whose large white flowers usually have eight petals around many yellow centre parts.
After flowering, each fruit grows a long, feathery tail; the leaves are glossy dark green above and covered in white woolly hairs beneath.
The name durian comes from duri, the Malay word for thorn, because of the fruit's spiny husk.
Durian flowers open at night and grow straight from the big branches, up to 30 in a bunch.

notes.PHL: Kew lists the durian as native in Borneo and Sumatra, and as brought by people to the Philippines.
notes.SGP: Kew lists the durian as native in Borneo and Sumatra; in the Malay Peninsula, including Singapore, it was brought by people.

facts.en: This bugloss is a shrub that grows wild on Fogo, one of the Cape Verde islands, and nowhere else.
An oil palm's fruit grows in heavy bunches: a typical bunch weighs about 23 kg and holds between 200 and 2,000 fruits.
Its genus name, Elaeis, comes from the Greek word for oil; in West Africa, palm oil is stirred into soups and sauces.
The name Elettaria comes from elettari, the plant's name in the Malabar region of southern India, where cardamom is native.
Known as the 'queen of spices', cardamom flavours food and drinks: Scandinavians bake with it, and in the Middle East it goes into tea and coffee.
Late summer is crowberry season in Greenland: the slightly bitter black berries are so plentiful in places that pickers scoop them up by the handful.
Crowberry is one of the dwarf shrubs that carpet Greenland's heaths; its black berries tell it apart from look-alikes such as blue heath.
Enset looks like a giant banana plant, but its 'trunk' is a false stem of overlapping leaf bases; it flowers and fruits once in its life, then dies.
In south-western Ethiopia, the starchy pulp of its false stem and underground corm is fermented in pits to make kocho, a staple food.
Its thick, curled seed pods look like human ears, which is why it is also called the ear pod tree or elephant ear tree.
Cattle, horses and wild hoofed animals eat the syrupy pulp of its pods and spread the seeds, while its wide crown shades pastures and coffee farms.
Its Greenlandic name, niviarsiaq, means 'the young girl'; it grows on gravel and rocky ground, dry heaths and old riverbeds.
A single stem can carry up to 14 flowers, each 3 to 5 cm across with four red-violet petals; white flowers are rare.
In northern Botswana this tufted grass of the Kalahari sands is cut to thatch roofs and to make brooms.
Its sturdy stems, up to 2 m tall, also form the core of coiled baskets, and farm animals seldom eat this hard grass.
Teff grains are tiny, just 1 to 1.5 mm long, so they are nearly always ground whole into flour, bran and germ included.
Teff comes from northern Ethiopia; in Ethiopia and Eritrea its flour is mostly made into injera, a thin, soft flatbread whose dough ferments for two or three days.
Its name means 'red' (Erythrina, from Greek) and 'rooster's comb' (crista-galli, Latin), after the colour of its big flowers.
The ceibo grows along the banks of the Parana and the River Plate, and its large red flowers have been used to dye cloth.
In Australia the river red gum grows along rivers and on floodplains, and it can stand waterlogging and floods that come and go.
The name Eucalyptus comes from Greek words meaning 'well covered', after the little cap that protects each flower bud.
Banjo Paterson's 1895 poem Waltzing Matilda, set to music the same year, begins with a swagman camped by a billabong in the shade of a coolabah tree.
Young blue gum leaves are broad and coated with a blue-grey wax, which gives the tree its name; older leaves are narrow and sickle-shaped.
Because it grows fast and straight, it has been planted widely outside Australia, including India, for its strong wood and for paper pulp.
A mountain ash lives 300 to 400 years; without fire, its seeds cannot grow up into new trees in the shade of the old forest.
A severe fire kills the trees but brings down masses of seed; if another fire comes before the young trees are about 20 years old, mountain ash can disappear there.
Pitanga's ribbed fruit turns from green to orange and then bright red or almost black, ripening just three weeks after the flower opens.
It is said that Portuguese sailors took its seeds from Brazil to India, just as they took the cashew.
The bright red, pink or white 'petals' are long-lasting bracts; the real flowers are tiny and sit in the middle of them.
Its name milii honours Baron Milius, governor of the island of Bourbon, who brought the plant to France in 1821.
A poinsettia's bright red 'petals' are really bracts, a kind of leaf; its true flowers are the small yellow cups clustered in the middle.
To colour up again for Christmas, a poinsettia needs long nights: from late September, about 16 hours of unbroken darkness every day.
Before dawn, Amazon river dwellers load baskets with pebble-sized purple acai fruit and bring them by canoe or boat to markets in Belem.
Acai grows in clumps of many stems, so palm hearts can be cut again and again from the same plant without killing it.
Buckwheat is not a grass like wheat: it belongs to the knotweed family, yet its cooked seeds are eaten like a cereal grain.
Buckwheat seeds sprout within 3–4 days, and its scented white flowers, blooming for up to three months, give nectar to honeybees.
Beech woods are so shady, with a thick carpet of fallen leaves and nut husks, that few woodland plants can grow beneath them.
Since the last Ice Age, beech has spread across Europe from a few refuges; old beech forests in 18 countries form one UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Its species name honours the German botanist Friedrich Sello, and both its flowers and its fruit can be eaten.
Hing is a gum-resin that builds up in the roots of this plant over about five years and is collected much as rubber is tapped.
India imports about 1,200 tonnes of raw hing a year from Iran, Afghanistan and Uzbekistan; in 2020, scientists began growing the plant in Himachal Pradesh's Lahaul valley.
The Great Banyan in Howrah's botanic garden lost its main trunk to a wood-rotting fungus in 1925, yet it still thrives on thousands of prop roots.
Gardeners guide the Great Banyan's young aerial roots down bamboo tubes, so each one roots where it will prop up a spreading branch.
Its leaves hang from drooping branches, hence the name weeping fig; it stays a slim pot plant indoors but can become a big strangling fig outdoors.
In Indonesia this fig is called beringin, and a beringin tree on the shield of the national emblem stands for the unity of Indonesia.
A fig is not an ordinary fruit: its tiny flowers grow hidden inside it, and many kinds of fig ripen without being pollinated.
Figs are eaten fresh, cooked or dried; in India, a single fig tree bears about 180 to 360 fruits a year.
Barbados may be named after this fig: Portuguese sailors who passed in 1536 saw its beard-like hanging roots, though some say the name meant bearded people.
Birds spread its seeds, which can sprout in the forks of other trees; the young fig sends a root down to the ground and may later strangle its host.
Its figs are bunches of tiny flowers turned inwards; a small wasp of its own, Pleistodontes froggatti, pollinates them and raises its young inside.
A Moreton Bay fig often starts life high on another tree, then sends roots down to the ground and slowly covers and replaces its host.
The peepal leaf ends in a long, thin tail that helps rainwater drip off quickly; engineers copied its shape to design a drip-irrigation nozzle.
Buddhists honour the peepal because, by tradition, the Buddha meditated and reached enlightenment under one at Bodh Gaya in Bihar.

notes.LKA: Kew lists the peepal (bo tree) as brought by people to Sri Lanka.

facts.en: Its long-lasting, almost rot-proof wood was used for roofs, furniture and boats; after heavy cutting, the tree is now protected in Argentina and Chile.
This evergreen conifer can grow up to 60 m tall and prefers wet, swampy ground where more than 2,000 mm of rain falls each year.
Ash wood is tough and absorbs shocks without splintering, so it is used for tool handles, oars and sports gear such as hockey sticks.
Ash dieback, caused by the fungus Hymenoscyphus fraxineus, makes ash trees shed their leaves as their crowns die back.
Each tall stem ends in a ring of drooping orange or red bells under a leafy tuft; imperialis refers to this crown-like circle of flowers.
In the wild it grows on rocky slopes, from western Asia to the western Himalaya.
The flat lobes at the tip of a mangosteen match the number of juicy segments inside, so you can count them before opening the fruit.
Its thick rind is dark purple outside and red when cut; in China it has been used to tan leather, and it gives a black dye.

notes.PHL: Kew lists the mangosteen as native in the Malay Peninsula and Borneo, and as brought by people to the Philippines.

facts.en: Tongans rank garland flowers by cultural importance, and the heilala's small red flowers sit at the top of that ranking.
Tongan tradition says the heilala came from Pulotu, the underworld, and its sweet-smelling flowers are strung into kahoa garlands.

notes.TON: Kew lists the heilala as native to Fiji and the Santa Cruz Islands, and as brought by people to Tonga.

facts.en: In French Polynesia, tiare petals are soaked in coconut oil to make monoi, a scented oil used in soaps, shampoos and skin products.
Visitors to French Polynesia are often welcomed with a garland of unopened tiare buds, and many people wear the flower tucked behind an ear.

notes.COK: Kew lists the tiare as native from Vanuatu and Fiji east to Samoa and Niue, and as brought by people to the Cook Islands.
notes.PYF: Kew lists the tiare as native to Vanuatu, Fiji, Wallis and Futuna, Tonga, Samoa and Niue, and as brought by people to French Polynesia.

facts.en: Ginkgo trees are either male or female; seeds from female trees have a foul-smelling flesh, so planters often prefer male trees.
Ginkgo leaves are fan-shaped and turn golden yellow in autumn; the name biloba is Latin for 'two-lobed', describing the leaf.
It climbs by the tendrils at the tips of its leaves, which cling to any shrub or tree they touch, and its stems can reach 4 m.
Its wavy, swept-back petals look like flames: the buds are yellow or greenish, and as each flower ages over about two weeks, its petals deepen to orange-red.
Soybean is native to East Asia; its species name, max, is Latin for 'large', perhaps after the size of its seeds.
Soybean is grown for oil and protein, for animal feed, and as a vegetable, edamame, whose green pods are picked when the seeds are plump.
Upland cotton supplies about 90% of the world's cotton, and its seeds give cottonseed oil, used in margarine and cooking oils.
Its large yellow or white flowers are followed by the boll, a capsule holding around 36 seeds wrapped in long and short fibres.

notes.IND: Kew lists upland cotton as brought by people to India from the Americas; India's old desi cotton is another species, Gossypium arboreum.

facts.en: Sturt's desert rose is a wild cotton: it belongs to the same genus as farmed cotton, though the hairs on its seeds are much shorter.
Its mauve petals have red bases that form a dark centre in each flower; the Northern Territory has it as its floral emblem.
It is called the tiger orchid for the tiger-like brown markings on its yellow flowers, about 40 of them on a stalk around 2 m tall.
This orchid grows on trees as a huge clump, with stems 3 m long or more; in Singapore it is grown on street trees.
As its blue flowers age they fade to paler shades, some almost white, so a tree in full bloom shows many tones of blue at once.
The wood is very strong and its natural resin keeps it slippery, so blocks of it were used underwater as bearings for ships' propeller shafts.
Its wood is so dense that it sinks in water instead of floating, and it was once used to make bowling balls.
Lignum vitae means 'tree of life'; this slow-growing tree copes with wind, salt and dry or wet soil, so it suits seaside gardens.
The guaria morada is an epiphyte: it grows perched on trees and other plants without harming them, unlike a parasite.
Heavy collecting has made it rarer in Costa Rica's forests, but it flourishes in many Costa Rican homes, where it is said to bring good luck.
Hagenia grows high on the mountains of Ethiopia and East Africa, about 2,000 to 3,000 m up, often forming woods just above the bamboo zone.
Trees are male or female; their drooping flower clusters, up to 60 cm long, are pinkish red on female trees and orange-buff to white on males.
The saxaul is a small desert tree, up to about 9 metres tall, with hard, brittle wood and tiny scale-like leaves; it grows on dunes and salty desert ground.
White saxaul is a small tree of sand dunes, up to about 7 metres tall, whose leaves are tiny scales pressed flat against its drooping twigs.
Because it binds sand well, China has planted it in the sandy regions of Gansu, Inner Mongolia and Ningxia, beyond its natural range.
Its name honours the Brazilian botanist Oswaldo Handro, and chrysanthus is Latin for 'golden flowers', after its showy, bell-shaped blooms 5 to 7 cm long.
Its wood is used for floors, building, veneers and sports equipment, and the tree is planted in parks and squares for shade and beauty.
In winter the yellow ipe drops all its leaves; in early spring the bare tree bursts into bright yellow flowers.
Ipe comes from a Tupi word meaning 'thick-barked tree', and its other name, pau-d'arco ('bow wood'), recalls the bows Indigenous peoples made from it.
Some lapachos drop all their leaves just before flowering, so their blossoms, from white to violet, pink and yellow, stand out even more.
Lapacho wood, especially from Handroanthus trees, is very dense and resists pests and weather, so it is valued for furniture and building.
Its woody fruits bear rows of arms tipped with hooked spines, which catch in the feet and hair of passing animals, so the seeds travel far.
Harpagophytum is Greek for 'grapple plant', and procumbens means 'lying down', as its stems trail along the ground.
Hedychium means 'fragrant snow', after the sweet-smelling white flowers; like ginger, the plant belongs to the ginger family.
Cuban tradition says that during the wars of independence, women hid secret messages in bunches of mariposa flowers.

notes.CUB: Kew lists the mariposa as native from the Indian subcontinent (India included) to Taiwan, and as brought by people to Cuba.

facts.en: Spanish travellers brought sunflowers from the Americas to Europe in the early 1600s; in Ukraine their oil grew popular because the Orthodox Church banned butter and lard during Lent.
After the 1986 Chernobyl disaster, scientists planted sunflowers to draw radioactive elements out of the soil and ponds nearby.
On the eastern Caribbean islands, its flowers are pollinated by the purple-throated carib hummingbird; their short, straight shape matches the bills of the male birds.
On Dominica, some of these heliconias have a second colour form whose flowers fit the long, curved bills of female hummingbirds.
Bolivia's decree on state symbols describes the patuju as a lowland flower whose long, sword-shaped parts carry bright red, yellow and green stripes.
Its bright, waxy bracts attract hummingbirds, which pollinate the small flowers tucked inside them.
Sundari is the main tree of the Sundarbans mangrove forest in Bangladesh, covering about half its area, and the forest's name is thought to come from it.
From about age three, sundari pushes breathing roots about 50 cm tall up out of the mud to reach the air; its hard red wood is used for boats.
Natural rubber is made from latex, a sticky white sap that flows when the bark is cut; collecting it is called tapping.
When its woody fruit dries, it bursts open with a bang like a gunshot, flinging its three seeds away from the tree.
Its hibiscus-like flowers open bright yellow, then turn orange-red and end up crimson as they age.
The name mahoe comes from a Carib word, and 'blue' refers to the blue-green streaks seen in its polished wood, which is used for cabinets and carvings.
Its Korean name, mugunghwa, means 'eternal blossom that never fades', and the old Korean kingdom of Silla called itself the country of the mugunghwa.
Its varieties are grouped by flower colour: baedal flowers are pure white, while dansim flowers have a deep red or purple centre.

notes.KOR: Kew lists the mugunghwa as native to southern China and Taiwan, and as brought by people to Korea.

facts.en: Its lemon-yellow flowers have a dark maroon centre; each opens for a single day and fades to pink before it drops.
Long strips of its inner bark are braided into rope, and its seeds stay alive after months afloat in seawater, helping the tree spread along coasts.
When Malaysia chose a national flower, people on the east coast picked the hibiscus and those on the west coast picked jasmine; the government chose the hibiscus.
It was picked because it was well known, had the same name across the country and was easy to find everywhere.
Its roots form nodules with Frankia, microbes that fix nitrogen from the air, so the shrub can grow on poor, sandy ground and is planted to hold sand dunes.
Its tart orange berries can stay on the branches all winter; the ancient Greeks are said to have named it 'glittering horse' and fed its leaves to racehorses.
Barley was domesticated from wild barley about 10,000 years ago; today about three-quarters of the world's barley is used to feed farm animals.
Barley copes with harsh conditions better than its close relative, wheat, so it can still give a harvest on poor, marginal farmland.
Bluebells spend much of the year underground as bulbs, and a seed takes at least five years to grow into a bulb.
People once used the sticky sap of bluebells as glue for binding books and fixing feathers onto arrows.
Its trunk forks into a Y again and again, so one doum palm can carry up to 16 leafy crowns.
Its fan-shaped leaves are woven into baskets, mats, brooms and ropes, and its hard seed, called vegetable ivory, is carved into buttons.
Holly trees are either male or female; the female trees bear the scarlet berries, which can stay on the branches all winter.
Young plants and low branches have prickly leaves that fend off browsing animals, while leaves high up on older trees are often smooth.
Wild yerba mate trees grow 12 to 16 m tall, but farmed plants are pruned to about 2 m, up to twice a year, to make picking easier.
The Guarani people used yerba mate leaves for a drink, in worship and even as money; Jesuit missionaries later began farming it.
Star anise is the star-shaped fruit of a tree from the mountain rainforests of southern China and northern Viet Nam; pods are picked just before they fully ripen.
Its sweet, liquorice-like flavour comes mainly from anethole, which makes up 80–90% of the spice's essential oil.
Its large, kidney-shaped seed must be cooked before eating; people roast, boil or bake it, or mash it into puddings.
The tree has a short, thick, deeply fluted trunk with thin buttress roots, and it grows well in swamps, marshes and along riverbanks.
Vesi's hard, dark red-brown wood, traded as merbau, resists termites and carves well, so it is prized for house posts, furniture and carvings.
Ancient Fijians held vesi sacred: it held up temples and chiefs' houses, and was carved into the lali, a wooden gong that announced important events.
It seems that Polynesian voyagers who had sailed to South America brought the sweet potato back to Polynesia.
Māori ancestors brought kūmara to New Zealand in the 1200s; as winters there are cold, they stored the tubers over winter and planted them out in summer.
It is known as a royal iris: each stem bears a single flower at its tip, and plants grow 30 to 60 cm tall, or taller in rainy years.
Its name comes from the village of Faqqua: the iris is widespread on the hills around the village.
In Jordan the black iris grows wild south of Amman, between Madaba and Karak; its rounded, almost black flower can be 12 to 15 cm across.
Its Latin name, nigricans, refers to its dark colour. Most of Jordan's wild irises are endangered, as building destroys their fragile habitats.
Croatia's name for the iris, perunika, is taken from Perun, the thunder god of the old Slavs; legend says irises grow where his lightning strikes.
The bearded iris is an ancient natural hybrid that arose in the Balkans; its name germanica comes from a mistaken belief that it came from Germany.
The name Ixora comes from Isvara, a Sanskrit word for God or lord, and coccinea is Latin for 'scarlet'.
This evergreen shrub is native to western and southern India and Sri Lanka; its bright red, four-petalled tube flowers grow in clusters.

notes.SUR: The faya lobi is grown in gardens in Suriname; Kew's checklist has no record of it there.

facts.en: The Isle of Man's ragwort code calls this native plant important for wildlife: it supports many invertebrates and is a major source of nectar.
Ragwort is the main food plant of the caterpillars of the cinnabar moth, a striking moth that flies by day.
Common jasmine is a climber of the olive family that can reach about 12 m; it grows wild from Iran and northern India to China.
Its pink to white flowers are so strongly scented that one vine can fill a whole garden with perfume.
Its Filipino name, sampaguita, is said to come from the words 'sampai kita', meaning 'I promise you'.
Arabian jasmine is grown from cuttings and layering, and its oil goes into perfumes, soaps and cosmetics.

notes.IDN: Kew lists Arabian jasmine as brought by people to Indonesia.
notes.PHL: The Philippines' national flower, the sampaguita, is grown in gardens there; Kew's checklist has no wild record of it in the Philippines.

facts.en: Its yellow or brown fruits look like tiny coconuts, with a nut-like shell marked by three 'eyes', and the seeds are eaten.
Found nowhere but Chile and rated Endangered, this palm was added to CITES Appendix I at Chile's request, which almost stops commercial trade in it between countries.
Juglans regia is Latin for 'Jupiter's royal nut'; the nut grows inside a green, fleshy husk that splits open as the fruit ripens.
Each walnut tree carries both drooping male catkins and small clusters of female flowers, pollinated by the wind; its crushed leaves smell like polish.

notes.KGZ: Kew lists the walnut as brought by people to Kyrgyzstan, not as native there.
notes.TJK: Kew lists the walnut as brought by people to Tajikistan, not as native there.

facts.en: Between 1946 and 1953, scale insects brought in by accident killed 95% of Bermuda's cedars; since the 1980s, seeds of the resistant survivors have been replanted.
Despite its name, the Bermuda cedar is a juniper; its soft red wood once built ships and furniture, and a seedling often tops a Bermudian wedding cake.
Juniper 'berries' are really cones that look like blueberries; they start green and take about 18 months to ripen to purple-black.
It grows across much of the northern hemisphere, usually as a low, spreading shrub on moors, rocky ground and in old pine woods; its cones are used as a spice.
Known in the timber trade as African pencil cedar, its scented, termite-resistant wood is used for pencils, fence posts, poles and furniture.
This mountain conifer often grows 30 to 35 m tall, with bark that peels in thin, papery strips; its name procera is Latin for 'tall'.
Its curved twigs droop, its grey-brown bark peels off in thin strips, and its name recurva refers to its curved-back leaves.
Himalayan weeping juniper grows on rocky ground at 2,500–4,500 m, where snow lies deep for long periods.
It is named after Robert Blossfeld, a German nurseryman who collected it in Madagascar and took it to Europe, where it became a popular pot plant.
It flowers after long nights: growers give it 14 hours of darkness a day for at least six weeks to make it bloom.
Its heartwood is a hard, dark red-brown timber, and the tree itself is an important street and town tree in West Africa.
Its round, woody fruit splits into four parts to release flat, winged seeds that the wind can carry up to 100 m.
Its sausage-shaped fruits hang on long stalks; one fruit can be 80 cm long and weigh up to 9 kg.
Its dark red, trumpet-shaped flowers overflow with nectar; fruit bats are thought to pollinate them, monkeys sip the nectar and antelope eat fallen flowers.
Its fragrant white flowers have a red throat, the colours of Singapore's flag, and their five petals are joined at the base.
In 1964 it was used in place of a ribbon at the opening of the rebuilt herbarium in the Singapore Botanic Gardens.
On Norfolk Island it is a common tree, growing over 20 m tall; its waxy pink and mauve flowers fade to white as they age.
The name copihue comes from the Mapuche word kopiwe, meaning 'to be upside down', as its bell-shaped flowers hang downwards.
Its red, pink or white flowers grow in moist forests of southern Chile, and Mapuche communities used to eat its berry-like fruit.
In northern Mongolia's forest-steppe, Siberian larch forests cover the cooler north-facing slopes, while the south-facing slopes are mostly steppe grassland.
Its thick bark shields it from ground fires better than the bark of the white birch, which often grows beside it in Mongolia.
The bay leaves of European cooking come from this tree; India's tejpat is a different tree, Cinnamomum tamala, though cooks use it in a similar way.
Bay laurel trees are male or female, and the female trees bear the fleshy black fruits; its name nobilis is Latin for 'noble' or 'renowned'.

notes.ESP: Kew lists the bay laurel as brought to Spain by people, though it is native in many other lands around the Mediterranean.

facts.en: English lavender is the source of true lavender oil, and its flowers are dried for potpourri; leaves, flowers and seed heads are all fragrant.
A dwarf shrub of the mint family, lavender needs very well-drained, rather dry soil in full sun and dies out in heavy, wet clay.
Henna dye comes from its leaves and young shoots, crushed to a powder; the orange-red paste decorates hands and feet with patterns and also colours hair, leather and cloth.
The name henna comes from the plant's Arabic name; its small white flowers are very fragrant and are used in perfume.

notes.SDN: Kew lists henna as brought by people to Sudan, not as native there.

facts.en: An edelweiss 'flower' is really 2 to 12 small yellow flower heads ringed by 5 to 15 woolly white leaves, arranged in a star.
Its name joins two German words, edel ('noble') and weiss ('white'); though linked with the Alps, it is thought to have come from the Himalayas and Siberia.
Māori used mānuka bark as a waterproof layer on roofs, and its poles for rafters, spears and paddle shafts.
Its genus name, Leucanthemum, comes from two Greek words: leukos, 'white', and anthemum, 'flower'.
In the 1800s it was taken from Europe to the United States, where it spreads as a weed of grasslands, roadsides and riverbanks.
The Bayahíbe rose is one of the few cacti with leaves, and its showy flowers look like roses.
It is critically endangered in the wild, so the Dominican Republic's National Botanic Garden and its partners have grown and planted more than 4,000 of them.
Steady trade winds bend the divi-divi's trunk and crown to one side, so on Aruba the trees all lean the same way, like natural compasses.
The tree is also called watapana on Aruba; its pods contain tannin, a substance used to turn animal hides into leather.
Its name formosanum means 'of Formosa', an old name for Taiwan, where this lily grows wild.
Its stems, up to about 2 metres tall, carry fragrant white trumpet flowers, often streaked purple outside; on Taiwan's north coast they open in April and May.
Stone Age lake dwellers in Switzerland seem to have used both the fibre and the seeds of flax, and linen made from flax wrapped mummies in ancient Egyptian tombs.
Linseed oil, pressed from flax seeds, has long been used to help paints, varnishes and printing inks dry.
The part of a lychee we eat is the aril, a juicy white layer around the seed, inside a rough rind that ripens pink to red.
Lychee trees need a spell of winter cold to form flower buds, then warm, humid summers to flower and ripen their fruit.
Coco de mer palms grow wild on two Seychelles islands, Praslin and Curieuse, and each palm is either male or female.
Its two-lobed nut can weigh as much as 18 kg; it takes about three years to sprout, and a palm about 25 years to bear fruit.
Ber tsetseg is a popular summer flower in Mongolia; it blooms for about three months, in shades from pale blue to light purple.
Mongolians decorate silver saddle plates with ber tsetseg, a flower that for them stands for tolerance.
Its white form is called monja blanca, 'white nun', because a small column at the centre of the flower looks like a nun at prayer.
A Guatemalan botanist said the white monja blanca had not been reported in the wild since 1992; he grows it to return it to the forests.

notes.GTM: Guatemala's monja blanca is the white form of this orchid, long called Lycaste skinneri; Kew's checklist names the species Lycaste virginalis.

facts.en: The macadamia nut has a smooth, hard shell 2 to 5 mm thick, and its kernel is more than three-quarters oil.
It is named after J. Macadam, who in the 1800s served as secretary of a scientific society in Australia, the Philosophical Institute of Victoria.
Mahua sheds its leaves from February to April, just when its musky-scented flowers appear.
In central India its fleshy flowers are an important food, because they can be stored for a very long time.
Its huge flowers, white to dark pink and 15–25 cm across, open on bare branches from late winter, before the leaves appear.
Trees grown from seed often take 20–25 years to start flowering, while grafted trees of named varieties flower in 12–15 years.
Its name denudata means 'naked': the large, scented, creamy-white flowers open on bare branches before the leaves appear.
In China it is called yulan, or 'jade lily', and it has been grown there since the year 618.
Its fragrant white flowers have red stamens at the centre; they open in spring and keep appearing now and then through the summer.
In autumn its pink fruits split open to show orange-red seeds, and its leaves turn golden yellow.
Today's apples very likely descend from wild Central Asian apples, Malus sieversii, which still grow in the mountain forests of Kazakhstan.
In the wild apple forests of Kazakhstan, bears eat the fruit and scatter its seeds in their droppings.

notes.KAZ: Kew counts the wild apple of the Tian Shan (Malus sieversii) as Malus domestica, native here.
notes.KGZ: Kew counts the wild apple of the Tian Shan (Malus sieversii) as Malus domestica, native here.

facts.en: New mango leaves come out reddish and slowly turn a shiny dark green.
Mangoes have been grown in India for more than 4,000 years; the tree is related to cashew and pistachio.

notes.BGD: Kew lists the mango as brought by people to Bangladesh, and as native in nearby north-east India and Myanmar.
notes.IND: Kew lists the mango as native only in India's north-east; elsewhere in India it was brought by people.
notes.PAK: Kew lists the mango as brought by people to Pakistan, and as native in north-east India, Myanmar and Thailand.

facts.en: Cassava roots can stay in the ground on the living plant for two years or more, so farmers dig them when needed; once dug up, they spoil within days.
Cassava was probably domesticated in the southern Amazon; Portuguese traders brought it to Africa in the 1500s, and it is usually planted from stem cuttings.
Buriti palms are male or female, and the male palms flower at the same time as the females but bear no fruit.
