Its trunk is used to build bridges and, because it floats, to carry other logs along rivers; its fruit feeds tapirs, peccaries and deer.
Bhutan's blue poppy was long counted as a form of Meconopsis grandis, until botanists showed in 2016 that it is a separate species.
It grows high in the mountains, at about 3,700 to 4,300 metres, and its name honours Bhutan's idea of Gross National Happiness.
Tagimoucia is a climbing plant of Fiji's upland forests; its bunches of flowers are bright red with white centres.
Fijians tell stories and sing songs about the tagimoucia, and the flower appears on Fiji's $50 banknote.
Its flower spikes look like brushes for cleaning bottles: the red colour comes from the many long stamens, and birds and bees visit the flowers.
Its old name, Callistemon, comes from Greek words meaning 'beautiful stamen', after its showy flowers.
A barrel-shaped cactus of coastal limestone and cliffs around the Caribbean, it bears bright pink, tube-shaped flowers.
Grand Turk's island colour, red, comes from this cactus's red-pink fruit; the cacti once grew thickly there before being cleared for salt ponds.
Ceylon ironwood is heavy and very hard, often blunting saws, and is used for posts, beams and heavy-duty floors.
Its showy, fragrant flowers each open for one day, from about 3 or 4 in the morning until around sunset.
Dawn redwood was known from fossils before living trees turned up in China in the 1940s, after the forester Gan Duo found a small group near the Sichuan–Hubei border.
A conifer that is not evergreen, dawn redwood sheds its feathery leaves each autumn after they turn coppery brown; its Chinese name, shui shan, means 'water fir'.
Its bright red flowers open around Christmas, so the pōhutukawa is known as New Zealand's Christmas tree.
In Māori legend, a small, 800-year-old pōhutukawa clinging to a cliff near Cape Reinga guards a sacred cave on the spirits' path to the next world.
Its trunk stores starch in its soft centre, and people extract it to make sago, still a staple food in some places.
A sago palm flowers just once, at the end of its life: after its huge flower head fruits, the trunk dies and shoots from its base take over.

notes.BRN: Kew lists the sago palm as native in Maluku and New Guinea; in Borneo, including Brunei, it was brought by people.
notes.MYS: Kew lists the sago palm as native in Maluku and New Guinea; in Malaysia it was brought by people.

facts.en: A few hundred of these cycads survive in the wild, in one small mountain area of Pinar del Río province in western Cuba.
Microcycas means 'small cycad', yet this one can grow into a tree up to 10 metres tall, and each plant is either male or female.
Iroko trees are either male or female, and the female tree's green, wrinkled fruit looks like a fat caterpillar.
Its hard heartwood resists termites and resembles teak; it is used for boats, furniture, floors and outdoor building work.
Moringa's long pods, the 'drumsticks', can grow 40–50 cm long; young pods are cooked as a vegetable and are said to taste like asparagus.
Moringa cuttings root easily, so lines of stakes are planted as living fences and hedges around houses and gardens.
It usually grows on mountain slopes up to about 800 metres, and in the UAE it is very common in the Ruus Al Jibal mountains.
White mulberry is grown on a large scale for its leaves, which are fed to silkworms, making it central to silk farming.
Despite the name, its fruits can be white, pinkish, purple or black; they are eaten fresh or made into juice.
A banana plant is not a tree but a giant herb: its 'stem' is a column of tightly wrapped leaf stalks.
Bananas grown for food, usually seedless, mostly belong to this species or to its hybrids with another wild banana, Musa balbisiana, which bears seedy fruit.

notes.PNG: Kew's checklist has no New Guinea record for Musa acuminata: it counts the island's wild form of this banana as a separate species, Musa banksii.

facts.en: Nutmeg and mace come from the same fruit: nutmeg is the kernel of the seed, and mace is the red, lacy covering around the seed.
Nutmeg trees are male or female, and growers cannot tell which a seedling is until it flowers, at around 7 to 9 years old.
This orchid grows on trees and sends up flower stalks up to about 1.8 metres long, with white and purple flowers that open around June.
It is native to the Cayman Islands alone: one variety grows on Grand Cayman, the other on Cayman Brac and Little Cayman.
The tree yields fragrant resins known as tolu balsam and Peru balsam; their scented oil is used in perfumes and soaps and to flavour baked goods.
In El Salvador its resin has long been gathered on the coast of La Libertad, known as the Balsam Coast, and the tree also shades coffee farms.
Its white petals surround a yellow cup with a red rim, and its flowers are strongly fragrant.
Its species name means 'of poets', and its genus is named after Narcissus, a youth of Greek myth entranced by his own reflection.
Compared with garden daffodils, wild ones are smaller and paler: a deep yellow trumpet sits in a ring of six much paler petals.
Wild daffodils have inspired poets for centuries, among them William Wordsworth.
A blooming lotus flower can warm itself, holding its inner temperature at about 30–35 °C for a few days even when the air is cooler.
Lotus leaves clean themselves: rainwater forms beads that roll off and carry dust away, which scientists named the 'Lotus-Effect'.
It makes two kinds of pitchers: reddish ones lower down and bright yellow ones higher up, which hang from coiling tendrils.
Madagascar has two pitcher plant species; this one grows along the island's east coast, at the edges of swamps.
Its leaf tips grow into pitchers that hold rainwater and digestive juices; insects that fall in are trapped and digested.
Some mosquito larvae live in the pitcher fluid, eating the plant's trapped prey and even each other.
Despite its name, the Guernsey lily comes from South Africa; plants grown on Guernsey have been sent out as 'Guernsey lilies' since about 1650.
Its flowers come in white, pale pink, deep red and purple, have a chocolate scent, and seem to sparkle in sunshine.

notes.GGY: Kew lists the Guernsey lily as native to South Africa's south-western Cape; on Guernsey it was brought by people.

facts.en: Harsingar's bright orange flower tubes hold a saffron-coloured dye, once used on silk and locally as a cheaper stand-in for saffron on Buddhist monks' robes.
Its fragrant white flowers with orange-red tubes open at dusk and fall by dawn, and the fallen flowers are strung into garlands as offerings.
It is a water lily with large white or cream flowers, 10 to 18 cm across, and round leaves with toothed edges.
Although called a lotus, it is a water lily (Nymphaea), a different plant from India's national flower, the lotus Nelumbo nucifera.
For years, Sri Lankan stamps and school books showed a violet garden water lily as the national flower by mistake; the true native flower is pale blue.
In Bangladesh, the flower stalks of water lilies are cooked as a vegetable, and the seeds can be fried until they puff up.
In many Hindu homes tulsi is considered sacred and grown in a decorated clay pot, often placed in the courtyard.
Tulsi leaves have a clove-like smell, which comes from a scented compound called eugenol.
Olive leaves are grey-green above and silver underneath; its small white flowers are fragrant, and its fruits ripen from green to purplish-black.
An olive branch is a symbol of peace; the fruits are picked green or ripe, to eat or to press for olive oil.
The pale maiden has slender stems and white, bell-shaped flowers with violet stripes, which open mainly in spring and early summer.
Legend says a barefoot Norse invader stepped on a thistle at night and cried out in pain, warning the Scots of the attack.
Scotch thistle can grow more than 2 metres tall, with broad wings along its stem and big leaves armed with sharp yellow spines.

notes.GBR: Kew lists the Scotch thistle as brought to Britain by people, not native there.

facts.en: People in Mexico, around the Mediterranean and in the Middle East eat its sweet fruit, called tuna in Spanish, and the tender young pads, nopalitos, are cooked as a vegetable.
Its flat pads carry clusters of three to six greyish-white spines, each up to 3 cm long, though some cultivated varieties have no spines at all.
African rice was domesticated in Africa from a wild African rice, separately from Asian rice; its grains are often reddish.
Many small farmers still prefer it to Asian rice for its taste and because it copes with floods; some floating kinds grow up to 5 m long.
Rice roots are built with air channels that carry oxygen to their tips, so rice thrives in flooded fields where wheat or maize roots would run short of air.
Inside its husk, each rice grain is 'brown rice'; milling rubs off the oily bran layer, leaving white rice.

notes.BGD: Kew lists rice as brought by people to Bangladesh, as a crop first grown in China.
notes.IND: Kew lists rice as brought by people to every Indian region, as a crop first grown in China.

facts.en: Its name says 'fragrant' twice: Osmanthus comes from Greek words for 'fragrant flower', and fragrans is Latin for 'fragrant'.
Its tiny white, yellow or orange flowers open in autumn, and just a few can scent a room; in China they are used to perfume tea.
Safou fruits look like large olives; their thin skin turns from pink to dark blue or violet, and the buttery flesh is eaten boiled, roasted or fried.
When its bark is cut, it gives a fragrant resin, used to seal calabashes and mend clay pots, or burnt like a candle.
Despite its name it is not a palm: Pachypodium means 'thick foot', after its thick grey stem armed with sharp spines in threes.
In the heat of its dry home it sheds its leaves, keeping small tufts near the top, where fragrant white flowers with yellow throats open.
In late spring it opens deep red, bowl-shaped flowers, glossy and about 12 cm wide, with a boss of yellow stamens.
Romania celebrates the peony, its national flower, every year on 15 May, and sees it as a symbol of its soldiers' courage.
Tree peonies keep their woody stems through the winter, unlike herbaceous peonies, which die back to the ground each autumn.
Peonies have been grown in Luoyang, a city in China's Henan province, for more than a thousand years; the tree peony 'Luoyang Hong' is named after it.
Pandan's female flowers have never been recorded and its male flowers are rare, so the plant is not known to bear fruit.
The leaves are not eaten: their juice gives cakes, kueh and teas a sweet smell and a green colour, and the leaf is removed before serving.
Kewda's fragrant male flowers are distilled into kewra water and kewda oil, which are used as perfumes.
It is a small, branching tree propped up by brace roots, with rosettes of long, stiff, spiny, bluish-green leaves.
Pandanus plants are either male or female; a female plant bears fruit heads made of many wedge-shaped pieces called keys.
On atolls, pandanus is valued next after the coconut: people eat the fruit of sweet varieties and weave the leaves into fine mats.
Each corn poppy flower lasts just one day, but the plant keeps opening new red blooms through spring and summer.
Poppy seeds can stay alive in the soil for decades; poppies growing on World War I battlefields made the flower a symbol of remembrance.

notes.GBR: Kew lists the common poppy as brought to Britain by people, though it is native in much of mainland Europe.

facts.en: This orchid is a hybrid: Agnes Joaquim crossed two orchids, Papilionanthe teres and Papilionanthe hookeriana, and it is named after her.
It can flower all year round in Singapore, but its long, thin stems need to be tied to a post for support.
Its seeds are fermented into dawadawa, a dark, strong-smelling seasoning that cooks crumble into soups and stews.
The genus honours Mungo Park, a Scottish explorer who travelled deep into West Africa twice, between 1795 and 1805.
It flowers in late winter, before its leaves open; the flowers have no petals, just dense tufts of red stamens.
In autumn its leaves turn red, orange and yellow, and the bark of older trees flakes away in patches of green, tan and white.
Passion fruit comes in two forms, purple and yellow; in Brazil the purple is preferred for eating fresh and the yellow for juice.
In India, purple passion fruit has long been grown in the Nilgiris and parts of the north, and in many areas the vine now grows wild.
Pau-brasil wood is rich in a red dye and was traded heavily from the early 1500s; today it is also used to make violin bows.
It grows wild in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, and its species name, echinata, refers to the prickles on its branches.
Guarana sodas, made from the plant's seeds, have sold by the millions in Brazil, where the drink is still a key part of national identity.
The Satere-Mawe people of the Amazon helped domesticate guarana, pounding its seeds into a paste that they shaped into round or long cakes.
Pemphis forms dense thickets on rocky and sandy shores and at the edges of mangroves, where high tide half-covers it.
Its extremely hard wood is carved into tool handles, fish hooks and pounders, and bonsai growers prize its gnarled, twisted trunk.
Its name Peristeria comes from the Greek for 'little dove': the centre of each waxy white flower looks like a tiny white dove, hence 'Holy Ghost orchid'.
Each year the mountain village of Las Minas, in Panama's Herrera province, holds a show in the orchid's honour; there it blooms from June to October.
Botanically, an avocado is a berry: one large seed wrapped in buttery flesh that is 3 to 30% oil, which is why it is also called butter fruit.
Avocado reached India in the early 1800s; it is grown mainly in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and Maharashtra, where ICAR has developed varieties such as Arka Supreme.
Its large white flowers grow along an arching stalk and last a long time; the lip has yellow edges and ends in two yellow tendrils.
It grows on trees, from sea level up to about 1,200 m, in forests from Borneo and the Philippines to New Guinea and Queensland.
Taiwan's wild white moth orchid grows in broadleaf forests 100–400 metres up, from the Hengchun Peninsula in the south to Taitung and Orchid Island (Lanyu).
Moth orchids in Taiwan have become scarce in the wild because people picked them for their beauty; this one has also been an important parent of new orchid varieties.
The common bean is native to the tropical Americas, where people domesticated it long before Columbus; hundreds of varieties have been bred since.
Bean plants put nitrogen back into the soil; some grow as climbing pole beans on supports, others as compact bush beans.

notes.BRA: Kew's checklist does not list the common bean as growing wild in Brazil; it appears here as a farmed crop.

facts.en: The Cape Verde date palm grows wild in the Cape Verde islands and nowhere else.
Some botanists have listed it under the common date palm, but a 2025 study found a feature of its anatomy that sets it apart.
Date palms are male or female: growers keep about one male for every 50 females and tie sprigs of its flowers into the female clusters, an ancient practice.
Dates ripen in four named stages: kimri (green and hard), khalal (yellow or red), rutab (half-ripe and soft) and tamar (fully ripe).

notes.DZA: Kew lists the date palm as brought by people to Algeria; it is native from Iraq and Iran to Arabia and southern Pakistan.
notes.JOR: Kew lists the date palm as brought by people to Jordan; it is native from Iraq and Iran to Arabia and southern Pakistan.
notes.MRT: Kew lists the date palm as brought by people to Mauritania; it is native from Iraq and Iran to Arabia and southern Pakistan.

facts.en: Harakeke is native to New Zealand and Norfolk Island; its flower stalks can reach 5 m and carry tubular, mostly dull red flowers.
Māori women scraped the leaves with a sharp shell to get a strong fibre called muka, which was made into nets, ropes, cords and footwear.
This shrub or tree grows wild in two far-apart places and nowhere else: the Tristan da Cunha islands in the South Atlantic and Amsterdam Island.
Moso bamboo is native to China; it was brought to Japan in the 1700s (in 1728 or 1736) and planted for food and timber.
Young moso stems can grow almost 30 cm in a single day, and even faster in hot countries; in Japan people cook and eat the young shoots.
The ombu is a fast-growing evergreen; its broad trunk swells into big outgrowths at the base, and its crown is wider than the tree is tall.
Ombu plants are either male or female; female trees bear lobed fruits, 10 to 12 mm wide, that ripen dark red to almost black.
Norway spruce is widely used as a Christmas tree, and its wood goes into roof beams, floors, furniture, boxes and paper.
Every year since 1947, the city of Oslo has sent a Norway spruce to London's Trafalgar Square to thank Britain for its help in the Second World War.

notes.BEL: Kew lists Norway spruce as brought to Belgium by people, not native there.
notes.LUX: Kew lists Norway spruce as brought to Luxembourg by people, not native there.

facts.en: Serbian spruce grew across Europe millions of years ago, but after the Ice Ages it survived just in a small area around the Drina river in Serbia and Bosnia.
Its narrow, spire-like shape and tolerance of poor soil and polluted air make it a popular garden tree in Europe and North America.
This spruce can reach 60 metres, with a narrow, pointed crown hung with drooping branches; trees that tall grow in the area south of Almaty.
It is named after the botanist Alexander von Schrenk, who collected the specimen it was described from in today's Kazakhstan; some trees are over 400 years old.
Allspice got its name because the dried berries taste like a mix of cinnamon, clove, nutmeg and pepper; it is also called Jamaica pepper.
The spice is made from the tree's berries, picked unripe and then dried; India grows some allspice too, on a small scale.
Caribbean pine copes with salty sea winds, so it can grow near the coast, and it is fairly good at surviving fires.
In Sri Lanka, Caribbean pine was planted to cover badly eroded land, and its trees are tapped for resin to make turpentine.
Known as sonamu in Korea and aka-matsu in Japan, this pine has reddish bark that peels away in papery flakes and plates.
Fire usually kills red pines, but new ones quickly take over burnt ground; in Japan the tree spread widely as farming spread.
Chilgoza pine grows high in the mountains, at about 2,000–3,350 m, on dry, sunny slopes with open vegetation.
Its oil-rich seeds, the chilgoza nuts, are prized as a dry fruit and are the tree's main use.
It is named after Aleppo in Syria, where the species was described, and is so drought-hardy that it is planted along highways without watering.
It grows in hot, dry places where forest fires are frequent, and it is planted to hold soil against erosion and to act as a windbreak.
Named after Huangshan, the 'Yellow Mountains' of Anhui where botanists described it, this pine gives that World Heritage site much of its famous look.
It grows on sunny ridges and open slopes of sandy, acidic mountains across eastern and southern China, from 600 to 3,400 metres up.
Oocarpa comes from the Greek for 'egg' and 'fruit', after its egg-shaped cones; its resin-rich wood, called ocote, is used to kindle fires.
This pine grows from Mexico to north-western Nicaragua and is abundant in the forests of Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua, where it is an important timber tree.
Chir pine often forms pure forests on dry, fire-prone Himalayan slopes; grown trees withstand fire fairly well, and young pines spring up fast after a fire.
Its slender needles, 20–35 cm long, grow in bundles of three, and its trunk is tapped for resin, an important product of Himalayan forests.
Ontario made the eastern white pine its official tree in 1984; the province has relied heavily on its timber since pioneer days.
Vast old white pine forests were mostly cut down by the late 1800s; today this fast-growing pine is planted for new forests, gardens and Christmas trees.
On older Scots pines the bark is orange-red near the top of the trunk and darker brown towards the base, which makes the tree easy to spot.
Its strong timber is used for building, poles and fences; the trunk yields resin for turpentine, and tar can be made from its roots.
Blue pine needles grow in bundles of five, 15–20 cm long, slender and usually drooping, with bluish-white lines along one side.
Chemicals released by its needles stop seeds from sprouting, so few plants grow under blue pines.
Black and white pepper come from the same vine: black is the unripe fruit dried whole, while white is the ripe fruit with its outer layer removed.
Pepper's traditional home is the Malabar Coast of south-west India, and the ancient Greeks and Romans already knew this spice well.

notes.IND: Kew lists black pepper as native only in Sri Lanka, and as brought by people to India.

facts.en: Its sticky seeds cling to the feathers of seabirds, which carry them long distances to other islands.
On coral islands it can form groves of its own, where seabirds such as the black noddy roost and nest.
Pistachio trees are usually male or female and are pollinated mostly by the wind; their fruits grow in clusters and tend to split open on one side.
Pistachio is a small tree, related to the cashew, rarely over 9 metres tall; its kernels are eaten roasted and go into sweets such as baklava and halva.
Its flowers and grape-like purple fruits grow straight from the trunk and big branches, which is what its name cauliflora refers to.
The name jabuticaba comes from a Tupi word for turtle, probably after the fat-like feel of its white pulp; seedlings may take 8 to 10 years to fruit.
Frangipani grows easily from cuttings: a branch tip left to dry for two weeks can be planted, and it may flower within a year.
Its fragrant, waxy flowers grow in clusters of 50 to 60, some with over 200, and are used to make leis and hair decorations.

notes.LAO: In Laos, dok champa (frangipani) is known as the national flower; the name covers the genus Plumeria, not one species. It is grown in gardens there; Kew's checklist does not list it in Laos.
notes.MNP: The 1979 law naming the flores mayo calls it Plumeria acuminata, a name Kew counts as Plumeria rubra.

facts.en: Cook's tussock grass is a perennial grass that grows wild on sub-Antarctic islands and nowhere else.
On South Georgia, tussac grass forms thick coastal grasslands where birds nest and many native invertebrates live.
In the Falkland Islands it grows along the coast and is the main plant on some small islands, giving shelter to many creatures.
The real yellowwood is a conifer with separate male and female trees; on female trees, round seeds sit on fleshy stalks that turn purple and feed pigeons and turacos.
Its yellow wood was so prized for floors, tables and cupboards that yellowwoods nearly vanished from some areas; they are now protected in South Africa.
Tōtara grows up to 40 m tall all over New Zealand; Māori chose its strong, straight trunks to build waka taua, their war canoes.
Māori used tōtara bark to make roofs and containers for food and water called pātua.
Around April its branches are lined along their whole length with bright scarlet flowers.
It is a hardy plant of dry coastal areas; grown high up in the hills, it becomes bushy but flowers much less.
An aspen grove is often one clone: new trunks sprout as suckers from the roots, and even year-old seedlings can do this.
Aspen grows from Newfoundland and Labrador right across Canada to Alaska; its light, soft wood is used for lumber, wooden matches and pulp.
Its purple to mauve-blue flowers, each with a yellowish throat, grow in tight, round heads on stout stems 3–15 cm tall.
It grows in the Himalaya from Afghanistan to Myanmar at 1,500–4,500 m, and its leaves keep growing after flowering, reaching up to 30 cm.
The Scottish primrose grows wild nowhere in the world but a small area of northern Scotland: Caithness, Sutherland and Orkney.
Its flowers are about 8 mm across, with five heart-shaped violet petals around a yellow centre, and it can flower twice a year, in early spring and summer.
Its one-sided clusters of bell-shaped yellow flowers were thought to look like a bunch of keys, so it has been called 'St Peter's keys'.
Cowslip flowers give early nectar to bees, beetles and butterflies, and the plant feeds the caterpillars of the Duke of Burgundy butterfly.
Primroses can flower from December right through to May, opening pale yellow flowers with five notched petals and a darker centre.
Primroses were the favourite flowers of the British prime minister Benjamin Disraeli, and Queen Victoria used to send them to him.
Kerguelen cabbage grows wild on a handful of islands in the far southern Indian Ocean: Kerguelen, the Crozets, Marion, Prince Edward, Heard and McDonald.
The ghaf grows new leaves, flowers and pods in the driest months, when other plants are bare, and stays green even in harsh desert.
In India this tree is the khejri; in the Thar desert its pods are cooked as a vegetable, fresh or dried.
Its lip is shaped like one half of a clamshell and is such a deep purple-brown that it looks almost black, which gives the black orchid its name.
Perched on trees in damp places, it can flower almost all year; its petals and sepals are greenish-yellow, spotted with purple at the base.

notes.BLZ: Belize's sources call the black orchid Encyclia cochleata, an older name; Kew's checklist names it Prosthechea cochleata.

facts.en: Each king protea 'flower' is really a head of many small flowers ringed by large, colourful bracts, and a head can be 12 to 30 cm across.
It survives the wildfires of its home with a thick underground stem full of sleeping buds, which send up new shoots after a fire.
Though people call it a nut, an almond is really a seed, held in a hard shell inside the fruit.
Almond trees flower early in the year, with fragrant pale pink to white blossoms that need insects to carry pollen from tree to tree.

notes.ARM: Kew lists the almond as a farmed plant (a cultigen) that arose in the Transcaucasus, which includes Armenia.
notes.AZE: Kew lists the almond as a farmed plant (a cultigen) that arose in the Transcaucasus, which includes Azerbaijan.

facts.en: Apricot flowers are white tinged with red and open early in spring; the fruit is ready about 70 to 100 days after the trees bloom.
Roman writers called apricots 'Armenian apples', the source of the name armeniaca; in Armenia, apricot wood is used to make the duduk, a musical instrument.

notes.ARM: Kew lists the apricot as brought by people to Armenia; its wild range is Central Asia and China.
notes.TUR: Kew lists the apricot as brought by people to Turkey; its wild range is Central Asia and China.

facts.en: Its deep red, bell-shaped flowers open in clusters on bare branches in late winter or early spring, before the leaves appear.
Birds love its small, shiny scarlet fruits; in parts of New Zealand, where it was planted in gardens, it has become a pest plant.
The plum is a hybrid: in the Caucasus the sloe and the cherry plum cross, and plants with doubled chromosomes gave rise to today's plums.
Damsons, a kind of plum, are named after Damascus, where they have been grown since before the Christian era.
Yamazakura, the wild mountain cherry, opens its reddish-brown young leaves at the same time as its light red or white flowers, in early April.
Wild yamazakura trees flower at about the same time as Somei Yoshino cherries, but not all together: some open a little early, others a little late.
It flowers in late winter: fragrant blossoms open on bare branches, and the leaves come out afterwards.
Although its blossom is called plum blossom, the tree is also known as Japanese apricot, and its fuzzy yellow-green fruits taste sour.

notes.TWN: Kew lists the plum blossom as native to south-central China, Laos and Viet Nam, and as brought by people to Taiwan.

facts.en: Peaches come from China, where people farmed them for thousands of years before the fruit became known in western Europe.
A nectarine is simply a peach with a smooth skin: both belong to the same species, Prunus persica.
Douglas fir cones, 8 to 10 cm long, have three-pointed bracts that stick out between their scales and turn brown when the seeds are ripe.
A major timber tree, Douglas fir has grown in western North America's forests since the middle of the Pleistocene ice ages.
Its buds wait until many are ready, then open together; each flower lasts a single day, so the tree blooms in short bursts.
Pterocarpus means 'winged fruit': its flat, round pods have a wing around the edge, so they ride the wind and can also float.

notes.MMR: In Myanmar, the name padauk is also used for a close relative, Pterocarpus macrocarpus.

facts.en: Native to the southern Eastern Ghats of India, red sanders has heartwood coloured deep red by a pigment called santalin.
Its dense, resonant wood is used for parts of stringed instruments, such as veena bridges and violin bows.
The name pomegranate means 'seeded apple': each fruit, roughly as big as a large orange, is packed with seeds in sweet-sour, juicy pulp.
Desert caravans once carried pomegranates for their thirst-quenching juice, and the fruit reached central and southern India from Iran around the 1st century CE.
White oak wood has long been split into staves for barrels, which earned it the nickname stave oak, and its acorns feed many kinds of wildlife.
White oak acorns ripen about 120 days after pollination and sprout almost as soon as they land, in September or October.
The golden oak is endemic to Cyprus: it grows wild in the island's Troodos Mountains.
This evergreen oak can be a shrub or a small tree of up to 10 metres; it is named for the golden undersides of its leaves.
'Sessile' means stalkless: this oak's acorns sit right on the twig, while its leaves have long stalks, the reverse of the English oak.
The oak was sacred to Zeus, Jupiter and the Celtic god Dagda, all gods of thunder; oaks are often struck by lightning as they stand tall.
Also called pedunculate oak, it carries its acorns on long stalks, while its leaves have tiny stalks or none.
An oak may need up to 150 years of growth before its wood is ready for building.
Brown oak acorns take about 15 months to ripen, and in Nepal, unlike other oaks, it ripens them in the middle of the monsoon rains.
Bears are fond of its acorns, and its leaves are a preferred food for silkworms reared on oaks.
Cork is the oak's thick outer bark: once a tree is 25 years old, the cork can be peeled off every 9 to 12 years and grows back.
Its thick, insulating bark shields the tree from wildfires, and a single cork oak can live about 200 years and be harvested more than 16 times.
Rafflesia has no leaves, stems or roots: it lives as strands inside Tetrastigma vines and is seen when its cabbage-like buds push out through the bark.
Its flower smells of rotting meat, drawing flies that carry its sticky pollen, sometimes for several miles, to another flower.
Raffia fibre is the thin top skin of young leaflets, peeled off and dried; soft but strong, it is used for tying plants and weaving mats, baskets and hats.
Its feather-shaped leaves can reach 20 m, and each stem flowers and fruits once at the end of its life.
In Madagascar its main pollinators are lemurs, such as the black lemur, which feed on the plentiful nectar of flowers that open at night.
Its leaves stand in two rows like a giant fan; travellers are said to have drunk rainwater caught in the leaf bases, though it is often unfit to drink.
Arfaj is a hardy desert shrub with bright yellow flowers and thorny branches; its roots help hold shifting sand in place.
Herders long valued arfaj as protein-rich grazing for camels and as a firewood that burns cleanly.
Noble rhubarb is called a glasshouse plant: its see-through bracts let light in and keep the flowers warm, while blocking ultraviolet rays.
Standing 1–2 m tall above the shrubs and low herbs around it, it can be seen from across a valley more than a kilometre away.
Its seed sprouts while the fruit still hangs on the tree; the seedling then grows for 3 to 6 months into a long, rod-like shape before it drops.
Fallen seedlings drift on the tides and can still take root after floating for as long as 12 months.
Its arching stilt roots grow out from the base of the trunk and prop the tree up, and air roots sometimes hang from its lower branches.
Its seedlings start to grow while still hanging from the fruit, as spear-like stems usually 36–64 cm long with a hard, sharp tip.
Its seed sprouts while the fruit still hangs on the tree, growing a long, pencil-like seedling 20 to 35 cm long.
Stilt roots up to 3 m long hold the tree up and soften the force of tidal waves, helping to protect the shore.
Its flowers may be red, pink or white, and a single cluster can hold up to twenty blossoms.
It quickly settles on freshly exposed ground, such as landslides and cuttings beside roads, and even grows in cracks in bare rock.
Called niau on Norfolk Island, this palm grows about 10 m tall, and its bright red fruit is a favourite food of the green parrot.
Early settlers ate its growing tip as a vegetable, made brooms from the ribs of its fronds and wove its fronds into baskets.
The nīkau has a ringed trunk, fronds up to 3 m long, pinkish flowers on spikes at the top of the trunk, and red fruit.
Māori used nīkau trunks for house posts or walls, its fronds for roofs and its leaves for weaving.
Its large greenish-white flowers smell of citrus, strongest in the evening; they open between May and August and each lasts about a week.
From 1946 until 1969 Honduras's national flower was the rose; in 1969 this orchid, which grows on trees in pine and oak forests, took its place.

notes.HND: Hondurans often call this orchid Brassavola digbyana, its older name; Kew's checklist names it Rhyncholaelia digbyana.

facts.en: Dog rose scrambles through hedges by hooking its curved prickles onto other shrubs, which hold it up as it climbs as high as 3 metres.
Its red, oval hips ripen in autumn; the hairs inside them are so irritating that they were collected to make itching powder.
After its flowers fade in late summer, the Carolina rose forms red hips that feed songbirds, quail, wild turkeys and small mammals through autumn and winter.
This wild rose of eastern North America spreads by suckers; its flowers draw bees and butterflies, and its leaves feed caterpillars of the Polyphemus moth.
Shaped by over a thousand years of breeding in Chinese gardens, these roses flower again and again on the same stems, so their Chinese name means 'monthly roses'.
This rose reached India early: it seems to have been common in Indian gardens by the late 1700s, and for a time it was even called Rosa indica.
Rose oil is costly: making one kilogram takes more than 3,000 kilograms of rose flowers, mostly Damask roses.
Damask roses give rose oil, also called attar of roses, as well as rose water, and they flavour food; the plant is a hybrid of three other roses.
The bases of the royal palm's leaves wrap tightly round one another, forming a smooth green 'crownshaft' on top of its pale grey trunk.
Royal palms shed old leaves on their own, about one a month; a fresh leaf can be 3 to 4.5 metres long and weigh up to 23 kg.
Cloudberry plants are either male or female; the berries start red and hard and turn soft, juicy and golden orange when ripe.
Cloudberries are hardly farmed at all, so nearly all are picked by hand in the wild, which makes them costly to buy.
Its bell-shaped flowers are carmine red with a white centre; in the wild it grows near Le Morne Brabant mountain in Mauritius.
It is rare, and Mauritius's National Parks and Conservation Service has raised young plants to put back into its natural home.
In old Lithuanian weddings, guests plaited a rue wreath for the bride as a symbol of chastity; later it was swapped for a married woman's headdress.
Rue has blue-green, fern-like leaves and clusters of yellow flowers, and its leaves feed the caterpillars of several swallowtail butterflies.

notes.LTU: Rue (rūta) has long been grown in Lithuanian gardens, but Kew's checklist has no record of it in Lithuania.

facts.en: Bermudians once wove the tough palmetto leaves into baskets, hats and fans, and also used them for rope and for thatching roofs.
Fossil palm fronds in Bermuda's coastal cliffs show that palmetto forests grew on the island for thousands of years.
In 1918, Coimbatore's Sugarcane Breeding Institute released Co 205, a cross of cultivated sugarcane with a wild relative; its 'Co' varieties are grown in India and other countries.
The word 'sugar' travelled from the Sanskrit sharkara through Persian and Arabic into European languages; sharkara originally meant grit or gravel.
Arctic willow hugs the ground as a creeping shrub just 5 to 20 cm tall, and its branches put down roots as they spread.
Its leaves have long white hairs underneath, and its male catkins bloom in June and July, their anthers turning from red to yellow.
Rain tree leaflets fold up in the early evening and on cloudy days, so in Malay it is also called pukul lima, 'five o'clock'.
In southern India, children have shaped the tree's ground-up seed pods into balls and dried them in the sun, making hard balls to use instead of cricket balls.
The quandong attaches itself to the roots of other plants with a pad-like organ called a haustorium, and grows better with a host nearby.
Its tart fruit, 2 to 3 cm across with yellow to bright red skin, is often dried and used in jams, sauces and pies.
Sandalwood is a partial parasite: its roots join onto the roots of nearby plants, so growers plant 'host' trees alongside it.
Its sweet-smelling oil, taken from the heartwood and roots by distilling, goes into perfumes and soaps.

notes.IND: Kew lists sandalwood as native from Java to northern Australia; it has been grown in India for centuries.

facts.en: Ashoka means 'without grief' in Sanskrit; in January and February the tree is covered in clusters of flowers that open yellow and turn orange, then crimson.
In north India the name 'ashok' is also given to a tall, narrow tree with drooping branches, the false ashoka; the real ashoka is also called sita ashok.
This carnivorous plant of nitrogen-poor bogs has pitcher-shaped leaves that lie on the ground, mouths open to the sky, lined inside with downward-pointing hairs.
Queen Victoria suggested putting the pitcher plant on Newfoundland's coins; in 1954 the province of Newfoundland and Labrador adopted it as an official emblem.
Bergfrue grows in rock crevices and on ledges, often where water seeps, and bears fragrant white flowers in large pyramid-shaped sprays.
Its thick, tongue-shaped, toothed leaves form big rosettes at the base, and Norwegians know it by many names, such as fjelldronning and fjellrose.
This beach shrub has fleshy leaves and pale yellow or white flowers; birds eat its round fruits, which turn from green to white as they ripen.
Its strong wood went into railway sleepers and its tannin into tanning leather; this heavy use in the 1900s has left the tree threatened.
In two of every three flowers fertilisation fails, so many of its winged fruits have no seed, which makes the tree hard to regrow.
The pepper tree has a drooping shape and soft, feathery leaves that smell strongly when crushed; its berries are shiny, pink to red and about 5 mm wide.
Marula trees are either male or female; the female trees bear the fruit, which is green on the tree and turns yellow after it falls.
People eat the fruit fresh or make it into jelly, and also eat the white nut inside; Sclerocarya means 'hard nut'.
Rye began as a weed in the wheat and barley fields of south-west Asia and grew alongside those crops for over 2,000 years before people farmed it.
Rye yields better than other cereals on poor, sandy or acid soils, and it keeps growing in the cool weather of late autumn.
Giant sequoias grow wild in about 75 groves scattered along the western slopes of the Sierra Nevada mountains in California.
Its cones can stay shut on the tree for 20 years or more; hot air rising from a fire dries them, releasing seeds onto freshly burned ground.
Foxtail millet was domesticated in China from a wild grass, green foxtail, about 9,000 to 6,000 years ago.
An ancient grain of northern China's Yellow River region, it copes well with drought and is also grown in India, where it is called kangni.
Sal leaves are made into leaf plates and cups, and they are also fed to the caterpillars that make tasar silk.
Sal's thick bark protects it from forest fires, and its hard, heavy heartwood resists termites, so it is used for railway sleepers and posts.
Goats eat argan fruit but cannot digest the hard-shelled nut, which farmers once collected from their dung to make oil; today machines often extract the nuts.
In long droughts the argan tree sheds its leaves and can stay dormant for several years; its seeds hold up to 50% oil, used in cooking.
With its clusters of strap-like leaves, the Bermudiana belongs to the iris family; in spring it opens purple flowers with a bright yellow centre.
It grows from beach dunes and rocky shores to coastal forest floors, and in lawns left unmown it can seed itself into meadows.
Although cooked as a vegetable, a tomato is botanically a berry, and tomatoes come in yellow, red and purple and in many sizes.
Tomatoes are native to Peru and spread around the world after Spanish colonisation; the word comes, through Spanish tomate, from tomatl in Nahuatl.
The potato comes from old local varieties bred by farmers of the Andes and southern Chile long before Columbus; these vary hugely in shape and genes.
A potato is a tuber, a swelling on an underground shoot called a rhizome or stolon, which grows from the lower part of the stem.
Kōwhai trees burst into bright yellow flowers in spring, and birds such as the tūī and bellbird feed on their nectar.
Eight kōwhai species grow in New Zealand; this one, Sophora microphylla, grows throughout both the North and South Islands.
Rowan is also called mountain ash because it grows well high up and its leaves look like ash leaves, but the two trees are not related.
People once planted rowans beside houses to keep witches away, believing that their bright red berries could fight evil.
Sorghum was probably domesticated in north-eastern Africa, perhaps in Ethiopia, a region where both farmed and wild sorghums show great variety.
Besides grain for porridge and pancakes, some sorghums are grown for a red dye in their leaf sheaths, used in Africa on leather, mats and cloth.
Its curved flower buds hold a red sap, and its big orange-scarlet flowers open in clusters, from the outside of each bunch towards the middle.
Its long, woody pods, up to 25 cm, split into two boat-shaped halves, releasing many flat seeds with thin wings that the wind carries away.

notes.KEN: Kew's checklist lists the Nandi flame as brought by people to Kenya; other sources, such as World Agroforestry, count it as native there.

facts.en: Cambodia's 2005 decree on national symbols describes rumdul flowers as white-yellow, with a scent that carries far in the late afternoon and evening.
For its scent, the rumdul flower is compared to Khmer women, and songs such as Rumdul Pursat are named after it.

notes.KHM: Cambodia's 2005 decree names the rumdul Mitrella mesnyi, a name Kew files under a related species; the rumdul grown in Cambodia is shown here as Sphaerocoryne lefevrei.

facts.en: Some accounts say Panama is named after this tree, which can grow 40 m tall on buttress roots and has large lobed leaves.
People eat its roasted seeds, which are said to taste like peanuts, and in Mexico the seeds are ground into hot chocolate drinks for flavour.
Each flower stalk ends in a boat-shaped sheath, from which 4 to 6 flowers with orange sepals and blue petals emerge one after another.
Strelitzia honours Queen Charlotte, wife of King George III, who came from the house of Mecklenburg-Strelitz; reginae means 'of the queen'.
Neelakurinji plants flower together once every 12 years; one Nilgiris family recorded the blue blooms in 1850, 1862, 1874 and on to 1922.
When neelakurinji blooms across the hills, the flowers draw big swarms of bees.
Despite its name japonicum ('of Japan'), the scholar tree comes from China; it was called the Japanese pagoda tree because it was planted at Buddhist temples in Japan.
A yellow dye can be made from its flower buds, and old Japanese prints were coloured with it; its creamy-white flowers open in large clusters in summer.
William Dampier collected a specimen in 1699 on an island off north-western Australia; it is still kept in a herbarium in Oxford.
Its flowers are usually blood red, with a shiny black bulge, called the boss, at the base of the top petal.
Each mahogany seed has a thin wing that makes it spin as it falls, so the wind can carry it up to 500 m away from its parent.
A mahogany tree stands above the shield on Belize's coat of arms, a reminder that mahogany logging was the base of its economy in the 1700s and 1800s.
Its timber was shipped from Hispaniola, the island of Haiti and the Dominican Republic, as early as the 1500s; the heartwood resists rot and insects.
Its woody seed capsule stands upright and splits from the base into five parts, each releasing about 20 flat, winged seeds.
Cloves are the dried, unopened flower buds of this tree; their name comes from the French word 'clou', meaning nail.
Clove trees once grew just in Indonesia's Maluku islands; in the 1770s seeds reached Mauritius, and later Arab traders planted cloves on Zanzibar, Pemba and Madagascar.

notes.TZA: Kew lists the clove as native to Maluku in Indonesia and brought by people to Tanzania, where it is grown on Zanzibar and Pemba.

facts.en: In old Indian texts the subcontinent is called Jambudweep, the land of the jamun, said to be named for its many jamun trees.
Jamun is held sacred to Krishna and is often planted near Hindu temples; Buddhists in South Asia also revere the tree.
It often flowers in the dry season, when the tree has dropped all its leaves and is covered instead with large white to pink flowers.
Its long, thin pods split open to free many winged seeds, which the wind can carry 100 metres or more from the tree.
In the dry season, as its leaves fall, the tree opens large pink flowers, often on its bare upper branches before the lower ones.
Its flowers, up to 8 cm long, range from purplish pink to almost white, and its long pods split open to free many winged seeds.
Tahina flowers once in its life: it raises a huge pyramid of millions of tiny flowers, sets seed and then dies.
In 2006 a cashew-plantation manager and his family found it in north-west Madagascar; sales of its seeds later paid for a village school.
Taiwania is named after Taiwan, home of the tree botanists used to describe it, and cryptomerioides means 'resembling Cryptomeria', a conifer with similar leaves.
Its wood is easy to work and has been used for buildings, furniture, bridges, boats and paper; in Taiwan it is now an important plantation tree.
Tamarind pulp stays sour as it ripens because its tartaric acid does not fade; sugar builds up alongside it, giving the sweet-sour taste of chutneys and sauces.
Its wide, dense crown makes the tamarind a shady village meeting tree, but so little grows beneath it that tamarinds are planted as firebreaks.

notes.IND: Kew lists tamarind as native to Madagascar and the Comoros, and as brought by people to India.

facts.en: Its leaves push out salty water through glands; the salt crystals left behind soak up moisture from the air at night, and the leaves then take in that water.
Its name aphylla means 'without leaves': its leaves are just tiny scales wrapped around its wiry twigs.
Its Mexican name, ahuehuete, comes from the Nahuatl words for 'water' and 'old', after the riverbanks where it grows and its long life.
In Mexico City's Chapultepec park lie the remains of El Sargento, an ahuehuete thought to have lived 509 years, possibly planted by the ruler Nezahualcoyotl in 1460.

notes.MEX: Mexican sources call the ahuehuete Taxodium mucronatum; Kew counts it as a variety of this species, Taxodium distichum var. mexicanum.

facts.en: Yews are a common sight in English churchyards: at least 500 of them hold yew trees older than the church buildings.
Yew timber is strong and long-lasting; it was used to make longbows and tool handles.
The name Tecoma comes from a Mexican word meaning 'vessel flower', after its cup- or trumpet-shaped yellow blooms.
Its yellow trumpet flowers, about 6 cm long, have faint orange stripes in the throat; in the wild, hummingbirds probably pollinate them.
Teak leaves are about 30 cm long, and young ones can reach a metre; the tree sheds them for three to four months in the dry season.
Teak wood feels oily, and freshly cut wood smells a little like leather; builders value it for ship decks and docks.
Its name Telopea comes from a Greek word meaning 'seen from afar', because its crimson flower heads can be spotted from a long way off.
Waratahs survive bushfires by regrowing from their rootstock, and they flower again about two years after a moderate fire.
Before falling, its big leaves turn bright yellow and then deep red; young trees spread their branches in neat tiers, like a pagoda.
Its fruit has a light, corky husk that floats, so sea currents carry it to new shores; people also plant the tree for its nuts, which are eaten.
About 100 of these conifers grow wild on Malta; in Europe they are otherwise found mainly around Murcia in Spain, but the tree is chiefly North African.
People have used it for over 2,000 years: its resin dries into small golden drops, and ancient temples had rafters of its rot-resistant wood.
Cacao flowers sprout straight from the trunk, and tiny midges about 1 to 3 mm long are key pollinators.
Its genus name, Theobroma, is Greek for 'food of the gods'; its seeds, cocoa beans, are up to half fat, which is cocoa butter.

notes.CMR: Kew lists cacao as brought by people to Cameroon; its native range in Kew's checklist runs from Costa Rica south to the Amazon.
notes.GHA: Kew lists cacao as brought by people to Ghana; its native range in Kew's checklist runs from Costa Rica south to the Amazon.
notes.MEX: Kew lists cacao as brought by people to Mexico; its native range in Kew's checklist runs from Costa Rica south to the Amazon.

facts.en: Its red, hibiscus-like flowers can be up to about 16 cm across, and the tree flowers and fruits all year round.
Its oval green fruits hold up to 12 seeds; bats eat the fruit pulp and so spread the seeds.
Its pale yellow, hibiscus-like flowers last a single day, darkening to pink, purple or deep red before evening.
Its dense, dark heartwood can be carved in fine detail and has been made into bowls, figures, tools and small canoes since ancient times.
British Columbia made the western red cedar its official tree in 1988; the tree is central to the traditions of the Indigenous peoples of the Pacific coast.
Western red cedars often live 800 to 1,000 years, and their light, long-lasting wood is a favourite for roof shingles.
Its flowers hang in clusters and have a rich, heavy scent that draws bees, and the dried blossom is made into a tea.
In Slavic mythology the linden was a sacred tree, and in German folklore it stood for fairness and justice.
The word shamrock comes from Irish words meaning 'young clover', and people wear a sprig of it on St Patrick's Day as a symbol of Ireland.
When naturalists asked people across Ireland to send in shamrock, in the 1890s and again in 1988, the commonest plant sent was this small yellow clover.
Farmers grow red clover for grazing, hay and green manure; it fixes nitrogen, so it is often sown to improve the soil.
Despite its name, its flower heads are pink to purple rather than truly red, and they smell of honey.
Wheat was domesticated in lands stretching from Mesopotamia to India and is now grown worldwide; its Latin name aestivum means 'summer'.
Wheat is also sown as a winter cover crop, because it smothers weeds and its roots and leaves add organic matter to the soil.

notes.IND: Kew lists bread wheat as native in parts of India, though wheat is usually said to have arrived from West Asia.
notes.IRN: Kew lists bread wheat as native in Iran, within the region where wheat was domesticated.
notes.PAK: Kew lists bread wheat as native in Pakistan, within the region where wheat was domesticated.

facts.en: Young Himalayan hemlocks look like drooping bushes, which is why the species is called dumosa, meaning 'bushy'; grown trees reach 20–25 m.
Tulips were brought to the Netherlands in the 16th century, and they still do not grow wild there.
Turkey helped make tulips popular in Europe, and the tulip is a common design on Turkish tiles, textiles and carpets.
Greig's tulip has grey-green leaves streaked and spotted with purple or brown, and a single wide cup-shaped flower, usually red or yellow, with a dark centre.
It was named in 1873 after Samuil Greig, a Russian general who was once President of the Russian Horticultural Society.
Bilberry stems stay green under winter snow and feed wild animals; in spring its flowers draw bumblebees, and in late summer its dark blue berries attract birds and people.
Settlers in Finland once said 'own ground strawberry, other ground bilberry': land covered in bilberries belonged to nobody, so a new settler could claim it.
Lingonberries grow on inland heaths of south-west Greenland, where their small red berries taste sour and slightly bitter.
Its seed pods coil into tight rings or spirals like a spring, which gave the tree its name tortilis, 'twisted'; grazing animals eat them and spread the seeds.
A tough dry-land tree, it can grow where just 40 mm of rain falls a year, and many birds nest in its umbrella-shaped crown.
Outside its home forests, every vanilla flower must be pollinated by hand; the method growers still use was worked out by a 12-year-old boy in 1841.
Vanilla is a climbing orchid that clings to trees with fleshy aerial roots; its famous scent develops as the pods are steamed, fermented and dried.

notes.FRA: Vanilla is grown on Réunion, an overseas region of France; Kew lists it there as brought by people.

facts.en: Each flat-topped cluster of creamy-white flowers is ringed by larger, sterile flowers, and its red berries feed birds such as bullfinches.
In Ukraine the guelder rose is seen as a national symbol, and it appears in many folk songs, artworks and embroideries.
Its flower opens white at dusk, holds scarab beetles inside overnight so they pollinate it, and reopens deep pink the next evening.
Its floating leaves can be 2 m across, held up by air-filled ribs underneath; these ribs inspired Joseph Paxton's design for London's Crystal Palace.
In West Africa, cowpea beans are ground into flour and made into cakes, fried as akara or steamed as moin moin, and the young leaves are eaten too.
Cowpea takes nitrogen from the air and can leave 75 to 150 kg of it per hectare in the soil, which helps the next crop.

notes.BFA: Kew lists cowpea as native across much of tropical and southern Africa, but as brought by people to Burkina Faso.
notes.NER: Kew lists cowpea as native across much of tropical and southern Africa, but as brought by people to Niger.

facts.en: Shea butter comes from the nut inside the fruit; similar to cocoa butter, it is used as a cocoa substitute and in pastry, soaps and skin creams.
Farmers usually spare shea trees when they clear land, so the trees stand scattered across savanna fields of cereal crops.
Grapes were probably domesticated around 4000 BC in lands south of the Black and Caspian seas; growing them then spread to the Mediterranean, western Europe, India, China and Japan.
A grapevine climbs with forked tendrils that grow opposite its leaves; unpruned, the woody vine can reach 15–20 metres or more.
The chaconia is named in honour of Don José María Chacón, the last Spanish governor of Trinidad.
This forest plant is known for its long sprays of bright vermilion, which come into bloom each year around the anniversary of Trinidad and Tobago's independence.
A welwitschia grows just two long leaves, which split and curl in the desert wind as it ages; in Afrikaans it is called 'two leaves, cannot die'.
Welwitschia has no close living relatives: it is the single species in its genus and family, and it bears cones instead of flowers.
Its resinous wood smells of cedar and resists termites, borers and fungi, so it was prized for building, boats and roof shingles that weather to silver-grey.
Found wild just in Malawi's Mulanje Mountain Biosphere Reserve, this critically endangered tree is being replanted: one project put in more than 550,000 seedlings.
Chinese wisteria twines anticlockwise around its support, and over the years its stems can become twisted, massive and trunk-like.
In spring, hanging sprays of blue-violet, pea-shaped flowers up to 30 cm long all open at about the same time, before the leaves have fully appeared.
Fossils of the Wollemi pine date back 91 million years, and scientists thought it extinct until 1994, when a small stand of living trees was found in a remote canyon.
It has dark red, bubbly-looking bark and fern-like leaves, and each tree carries both male and female cones.
Its flower spike can grow up to 1.8 m long, and grass trees often flower in great numbers within two years after a bushfire.
Aboriginal people used the flower stalks to light fires and to take fire from one place to another.
The izote opens clusters of bell-shaped, ivory or cream flowers, mainly in April and May, at the tips of its tall stems.
Its flowers are a traditional food in El Salvador, cooked in stews; one family recipe blanches them and then fries them with scrambled eggs.

notes.SLV: Kew's checklist lists the izote as native from Mexico to Panama but as brought by people to El Salvador.

facts.en: Despite its name, the calla or arum lily is neither a true arum nor a lily; its white 'petal' is really a modified leaf called a spathe.
Its leaves can push out extra water through special pores, which helps it grow in marshes, from the coast up to 2,250 m.
Before black pepper arrived from India in the third century, Sichuan pepper was one of ancient China's main spices, along with ginger and Chinese cinnamon.
Sichuan pepper grown south of China's Qinling Mountains tends to contain more of the compounds that give the spice its numbing feel.
Maize is pollinated by the wind, so it is sown in blocks of several rows rather than one long row, to make sure the flowers get pollen.
Genetic studies show maize was tamed just once, from the wild grass teosinte, in southern Mexico some 9,000 years ago.
The ginger we eat is a rhizome, an underground stem: young rhizomes are juicy and mild, and they turn drier, more fibrous and sharper as they age.
Ginger flowers grow on separate leafless stems, and a newly planted clump does not flower for about two years.
Jujubes seem to have been domesticated in China's Yellow River region over 6,000 years ago, as farmers chose trees with larger, sweeter fruit.
Fresh jujubes are crisp like an apple; as they ripen further they turn brownish-purple and wrinkled, and taste like dates.

notes.IRN: Kew lists the jujube as native to northern and eastern China and Korea, and as brought by people to Iran.

facts.en: Its thorns grow in pairs, one straight and one curved; its Latin name spina-christi comes from its common name, Christ's thorn.
A very deep taproot lets sidr survive in deserts with as little as 100 mm of rain a year, and it is planted to hold sand dunes in place.
